chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Committee on Public Housing hearing and asks everyone to silence devices and avoid approaching the dais. Staff also directs anyone wishing to testify in person to fill out a slip outside in the hallway.
chapters.title: Council staff gives hearing instructions and sign-up details

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing from the Committee on Public Housing.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this point, I'd like to remind everyone to please silence your electronic devices and at no point is anyone to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to sign up for in-person testimony and haven't filled out a slip, please feel free to fill out one outside at the table in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we're ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Council Member Chris Banks calls the hearing to order and identifies himself as chair of the Committee on Public Housing. He announces an oversight hearing on work order systems used in NYCHA and PACT developments.
chapters.title: Chair Banks calls hearing to order and introduces NYCHA/PACT work order oversight

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'm calling this meeting to order.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to this hearing on the Committee of Public Housing for New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Chris Banks, Chair of the Committee, and I'm glad to be joined by my colleagues, Councilmember Marte and Councilmember Escarceon.

chapters.summary: Banks explains that residents use work orders to request repairs and notify managers of conditions. He notes NYCHA has separate systems for complaints and work orders, while PACT properties use their own systems, causing open work orders to disappear during transitions.
chapters.title: Banks outlines NYCHA and PACT work order systems and transition problems

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Today, we will hold an oversight hearing on the work orders systems used in NITRA and PAC developments, which

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: residents use to request repairs and notify property managers of conditions in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA has two separate systems, the CBO tracks and the residence complaint and the Maximo tracks that tracks the work order.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA uses work order data to schedule repairs, direct resources, and measure compliance with the 2019 HUD agreement.

chapters.summary: Banks says open work orders have risen and fallen across mayoral administrations, with one-time funding used to reduce backlogs before they rise again. He criticizes that NYCHA's public work order data only goes back one year, preventing residents from tracking trends.
chapters.title: Banks on work order backlog cycles and limited public data

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A number of the open work orders has risen and fallen across mayoral administrations.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In the past, the city has committed one-time money to bringing the backlog down each time before it rises again.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The work order system is the main way for residents to report that something in their household needs repair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But residents and the public have limited ability to see how the system performs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA's work or the system only serves developments that NITRA manages.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: However, each PAC property manager uses its own system.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So residents have complained that their open work orders disappear from the NITRA system and that the history of the issue does not carry over to PAC.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA's work order system serves only developments that NITRA manages.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When a development transitions to PAC, its work orders leaves NITRA system and are then tracked by private management.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It is unclear what happens to the open work orders at that point and whether NITRA keeps track or communicates with the PAC partners of their progress.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And NITRA's public data on work orders only goes back one year.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the public cannot track trends.

chapters.summary: Banks says NYCHA and PACT residents report repairs take too long and that they are not updated on request status. He adds that PACT residents are unsure where to call when property managers do not respond.
chapters.title: Banks on resident complaints about delays and lack of updates

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, residents of both NITRA and PAC developments have reported that work orders take too long to address.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: They wait for repairs without knowing when a worker will come.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And they tell us that no one updates them on the status of their requests.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, PAC residents tell us they are unsure where to call or where the property manager, when the property manager does not respond.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We need today's hearing to shed light on a process that has frustrated and confused residents who are trying to live in dignity.

chapters.summary: Banks says a properly managed work order system can improve residents' well-being within days. He calls for NYCHA accountability, transparency from NYCHA and PACT partners, and timely complete work orders regardless of building management.
chapters.title: Banks states hearing goals: accountability, transparency, timely repairs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A work order system that is managed properly can improve the well-being of residents within days.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So this hearing is our chance to hold NYCHA accountable while also learning how

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: PAC partners handle repairs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We're asking NYCHA and PAC partners for more transparency moving forward.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: As more PAC transitions occur, residents need a commitment to timely and complete work orders, regardless of who manages the building.

chapters.summary: Banks thanks committee staff and then calls up the pre-panelists, including Jeremy Estrada, Keith Ramsey, Mateen Sarisi, Carla Hollingsworth, and Patricia Dickey. He notes Patricia Dickey is joining by Zoom.
chapters.title: Banks thanks staff and calls first panel of public witnesses

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I would like to first of all thank my staff, Michael Lambert, Kyle Graham, along with the Public Housing Committee staff, Jose Conde, Samia Shell, Charles Kim, Spencer Trun, and James Wu and Noah Schlossberg

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: for all the work they've put into this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Next, we will now welcome, as we have done traditionally in my committee, since I've become chair of this committee, we will now call up the pre-panelists.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So please approach.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We have Jeremy Estrada Perez.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Keith Ramsey.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And methane, Scorsese.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we've also been joined by Council Member Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we also have Carla Hollingsworth as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we have Patricia Dickey, who's on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We will begin with Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Mathane Scars.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You have three minutes.

chapters.summary: Mateen Sarisi says he is co-chair of Manhattan Community Board 9's Housing, Land Use, and Zoning Committee and a NYCHA employee testifying in his personal capacity. He says NYCHA reorganization helped uncover disinvestment in work orders and HPD violations.
chapters.title: Mateen Sarisi introduces himself and frames NYCHA disinvestment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Banks, members of the Public Housing Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: My name is Mateen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Sarsi, and I serve as the co-chair of the Housing, Land Use, and Zoning Committee for Manhattan Committee Board 9.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: I'm also an employee of the New York City Housing Authority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: However, I'm testifying today in my personal capacity, and the views expressed in this statement are my own and do not reflect any official policy or position.

chapters.summary: Sarisi argues that property management operations are siloed, which helped uncover issues but makes repairs hard to coordinate. He advocates for multi-trade teams and community partnerships to address multiple apartment issues at once.
chapters.title: Sarisi says siloed property management causes repair delays

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: I think one of the unique things about my experience having come from city council is, you know, being able to problem solve issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And there was a period of time in NYCHA where I was directed to look at community centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And so I think one of the cool things about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: What NYCHA is kind of doing, at least on the Section 9 side, was a lot of their reorganization really helped to uncover the extent of the disinvestment at NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: not just in work orders, but also in HPD violations, which now exist online.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And there's a lot more information that tells us how bad the situation really is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Part of the problem that I kind of see and I saw, I don't know if it's changed in the three years that I was working on this particular project, but a lot of the property management operations are very siloed,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: which worked really well for uncovering a lot of the issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: But now when you actually have to address them, it actually becomes almost impossible just because now you have a unit with a variety of issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And if it takes a trade skill a certain amount of time for each one to follow up, yeah, you're going to see delays for about a year or more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And so one of the things that I think worked really well when we were doing community centers, and I've tried to pass on those notes, is what it actually looks like when we're working with a variety of people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And so just on the community center side, what it looks like to have trade skills, a variety of trade skills working on a location at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: With capital projects because there are things that capital projects does that operations doesn't know about and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And when you tend to have multiple teams in one room, you tend to see a lot of expertise come back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And if you use community partnerships, at least in terms of community centers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: There's collaborative ways that you could work with people to address a variety of issues.

chapters.summary: Sarisi says the app does not let maintenance generate multiple work orders and instead leaves residents to figure out repairs. He says the app is not connected to the property management software, creating gaps and making it hard to reach planning staff.
chapters.title: Sarisi criticizes MyNYCHA app and disconnected work order software

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Despite a lot of work order reform that's been ongoing, I'd say one of the bigger issues that we have is the fact that the app itself doesn't have a process for maintenance to actually produce a variety of work orders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Instead, it gives the...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Resident to, you know, essentially passing the buck for them to figure out their own repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: So they have to call a planning person who would manage about 3000 apartments if they're there, or if there's a position.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And then even within that planning,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: It's up to the resident to figure out the order and that planning, whether people show up in a certain time set.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And it doesn't seem like the app is connected to the software tool that's currently used.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 30 seconds to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And so as kind of a result of that, you know, you tend to have these like big gaps in the work orders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: A lot of the times there's not a real way to kind of like reach out to certain folks if there's somebody in the planning unit that's not there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: And so again, at the end of the day, my two biggest things are the fact that you don't have teams of multiple trade skills dealing with a variety of repairs at once and a software program that actually connects the app

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: to the property management system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mateen Sarisi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Now we're going to move to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Carla Hollingsworth.

chapters.summary: Carla Hollingsworth identifies herself as secretary of the Stuyvesant Gardens One Tenants Association. She says residents were promised major renovations through PACT but are experiencing serious failures instead.
chapters.title: Carla Hollingsworth introduces Stuyvesant Gardens One PACT concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Pull the mic a little closer, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Holmes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: My name is Carla Hollingsworth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: I'm the Secretary of the Stuyvesant Gardens One Tenants Association.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: I submit this testimony concerning conditions residents are experiencing during the ongoing pack construction at Stuyvesant Gardens One.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Our fundamental concern is simple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: What residents were told they would receive through this conversion greatly differs from what residents are actually receiving.

chapters.summary: Hollingsworth says residents returned to apartments represented as newly renovated only to be relocated again due to leaks, sewage backups, and falling ceilings. She asks why contractors continue moving apartment to apartment before determining why completed work failed.
chapters.title: Hollingsworth describes failed renovations, leaks, and repeated relocations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents were promised major renovations and improvements, yet work that has only recently been completed is already experiencing serious failures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents have temporarily relocated for construction and then returned to apartments represented as newly renovated and then had to be relocated again because of conditions including serious leaks,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: sewage backing up into apartments, falling ceilings, and other failures occurring during renovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: This raises a basic question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: If recently completed work is already failing, why are the contractors being permitted to continue moving from apartment to apartment without first determining why that work failed and whether the same problems are being repeated elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents should not become the quality control inspectors for a multi-million dollar rehabilitation project.

chapters.summary: Hollingsworth says residents attempting to open newly installed windows had frames fall inward onto them, after which they were told not to touch the windows. She asks who installed and inspected the windows and how many failures have occurred.
chapters.title: Hollingsworth questions falling windows and inspections

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Several residents have reported attempting to open newly installed windows only to have the window frame and all come inward and fall onto them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents have subsequently been instructed not to touch or attempt to open their windows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: A newly renovated apartment should not be considered complete if a resident cannot safely operate the windows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: We want to know who installed these windows, who inspected them, how many failures have occurred, whether all similarly installed windows have been inspected, and why construction is continuing before the cause of these failures has been addressed.

chapters.summary: Hollingsworth says residents were initially told there was no asbestos, but asbestos-containing material was later identified and encapsulated rather than removed. She calls for transparency about where asbestos remains, what was removed, and who inspected the work.
chapters.title: Hollingsworth raises asbestos encapsulation transparency

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents were initially told that there was no asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Nevertheless, asbestos-containing material has been identified, and residents have observed work in which asbestos-containing material is being encapsulated rather than removed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents deserve complete transparency concerning where asbestos-containing material

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: remains, what was encapsulated, what was removed, who performed the work, who inspected it, and what procedures will protect the residents and workers if those materials are disturbed during future construction or repairs.

chapters.summary: Hollingsworth says first-floor apartments were altered for wheelchair accessibility even where residents did not need accessible units, reducing usable space. She says residents were not shown altered floor plans and some returned to find their furniture no longer fit.
chapters.title: Hollingsworth on accessibility alterations shrinking apartments without notice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: A number of first floor apartments were altered to provide wheelchair accessibility, even though the residents occupying those particular apartments did not require accessible units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: We want to be

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Be very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Accessibility is not the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Accessible apartments are necessary and important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: The issue is what happened to the existing residents.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 30 seconds to wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Hallways were widened, bathrooms enlarged to accommodate roll-in showers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: As a result, usable space elsewhere in the apartments was reduced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents were not shown the altered floor plans beforehand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Some residents returned from temporary relocation and discovered that furniture and belongings that fit into their apartments before construction no longer fit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: One resident, after seeing her altered apartment, refused to return because she said that she can't fit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: She's being threatened that she will lose her subsidy if she doesn't go back.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You finished?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'll give you 30 more seconds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents should not discover permanent alterations to their homes only after the work has already been completed.

chapters.summary: Hollingsworth says ETC manages about 22 contracting companies at Stuyvesant Gardens One and residents cannot get answers about who is doing what or who is accountable. She disputes the claim that renovations cost $380,000 per unit based on apartment conditions.
chapters.title: Hollingsworth asks about contractors, ETC, and $380,000 per unit

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Residents also have repeatedly requested information concerning the contractors and workers performing construction at Stuyvesant Gardens 1.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: We have been told that ETC manages approximately 22 contracting companies working simultaneously at the development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: We've repeatedly asked, who are these companies?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: What work is each company performing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Who's responsible for supervising and inspecting their work?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Who is accountable when that work fails?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: We have gotten no answers to date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: Also, they keep telling us that it's $380,000 per unit to renovate our development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: And if you look at these apartments, somebody needs to look at these apartments because it is not...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carla Hollingsworth
utterances.text: If $15,000 goes into an apartment, that's a lot.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Carla.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So you can submit that for written testimony since you've been able to complete your full testimony, okay?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony again.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We are now going to move on to...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Keith Ramsey.

chapters.summary: Keith Ramsey says Eastchester Gardens implemented PropertyMeld so residents can submit and track work orders online or by phone. He reports 3,280 tickets created, 98% completed, a median response time of about 24 hours, and a 3.3-day average turnaround.
chapters.title: Keith Ramsey describes Eastchester Gardens PropertyMeld system and results

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Our priority in Eastchester is simple, to make sure resident repair requests are handled quickly, transparently, and thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: To achieve this, we implemented PropertyMeld, a platform that gives residents a familiar, streamlined experience, much like that NYCHA app.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Through property mail, residents can submit work orders directly from a phone or computer, track progress in real time, and message maintenance staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: At the same time, we ensure no resident is left behind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Anyone who prefers traditional non-digital methods can call or visit

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: the on-site office or contract the WaveQuest repair team, and the staff will log and track the request directly into the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: For them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: The data shows their approach is working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Since launching, property mail to East Chester Gardens, 3,280 work tickets have been created.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: 98% of those work orders have already been completed, leaving just 1% currently open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: The median response time to a request in East Chester Gardens is approximately 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Over the last 90 days, our average completion and turnaround has been 3.3 days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Most importantly, our residents are rating the service at an average of 4.1 out of 5 stars.

chapters.summary: Ramsey says residents receive automated notifications and can choose appointment windows, with every action timestamped. He also describes a joint RA Ledger with the Eastchester Gardens Resident Association that reviews open, stalled, or defaulted tickets every two weeks.
chapters.title: Ramsey on communication, accountability, and RA Ledger tracking

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: A major reason for these results is

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: better communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: When residents put in a request, they can select their preferred appointment windows and receive automated notifications at every stage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Every message, update, and action is timestamped and documented so nothing falls through the cracks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Finally, technology is only as good as the people behind it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Accountability rests with our on-site property manager and dedicated management team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Eddie Shester gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Supported directly by the Wave Cuts Repairs team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: They monitor and track tickets daily, follow up with the residents, and ensure repairs are resolved properly and promptly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: We're proud of the response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Times and responsiveness and the accountability we have built and we remain dedicated to continuing this high standard for every resident in East Chester Gons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Also, we have created a joint tracking system that's the first in this city with the New York City High, I'm with Wave Press, I'm sorry, Wave Press and the East Chester Gons Resident Association called

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: We call it, what's the name?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: It's called the RA Ledger Evaluation List.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: And what it is, every two weeks, we get open, stalled, or defaulted tickets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: And if there's a problem, we straighten those things out ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: So we get a biweekly list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Keith Ramsey
utterances.text: Ain't no New York City Housing Authority property manager ever gave us data on the open tickets.

utterances.text: We will now, Layla Glasgow, if you could approach the dais.

chapters.summary: Jeremy Estrada identifies himself as a housing organizer from Western Queens and says his mother lives in Brownsville. He says his mother was told in August 2026 that kitchen cabinets and a sink would not arrive until October 2026.
chapters.title: Jeremy Estrada testifies on mother's delayed kitchen cabinets and sink

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: Hello, ladies and gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I am very happy to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: My name is Jeremy Estrada.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I am a housing organizer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I have been a housing organizer for six years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I am from Western Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: My mother lives in Brownsville.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I would like to start with my mother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: You see, recently, my mother had gotten a work order done for her cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: This was done on August 20th of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: She was only given one phone call, which was an update, that she wouldn't be able to get her kitchen cabinets and sink until October 20th of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: This, as her son and as a organizer,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: really, you know, enraged me in a way because how are we going to, you know, how is my mother going to leave her dishes on the floor?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: Unfortunately, a lot of Nitro developments suffer with roach issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: And rodent issues.

chapters.summary: Estrada says NYCHA developments suffer from roach and rodent issues and need more repair funding and clarity for tenants. He describes testing a cracked floor for a resident and getting a positive asbestos result after a months-long work order delay.
chapters.title: Estrada describes asbestos test and calls for faster repairs and funding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I would just like to say that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: NITRA needs more funding to repairs and also needs more clarity to the individual tenants that live in NITRA developments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: From my personal experience, I have done a lot of things with Queensbridge houses, Astoria houses, and Ravenswood houses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: And I have seen quite a number of repairs that have not gone repaired in months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: One of the most shocking things that I have experienced was this girl who lived in her apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: And unfortunately, her floor was cracked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: And underneath those cracks was asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I bought a test kit for her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: And I tested it myself and it came out positive for asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: It is clear that, I mean, she put in the work order and she didn't get it until months later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I feel like we need to be more quick with repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: It shouldn't really take this long, especially with something as minor as cabinets to something as serious as asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeremy Estrada
utterances.text: I yield my time.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We'll now go to, and thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We will now go to Patricia.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Patricia Dickey, who's on via Zoom.

chapters.summary: Patricia Dickey says work orders are often incomplete, delayed for months, or closed after workers claim she was not home. She says residents are sometimes left to do repairs themselves or manage without service.
chapters.title: Patricia Dickey describes delayed and closed-out work orders at Pink Houses

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Good afternoon, committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: My name is Patricia Dickey, and I reside in housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And when it comes to work orders, it's half of the time they're not completed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: It's a long delay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: You have to sometimes get tickets closed out to get the work that you need right then and there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: There's months apart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: When you need work, if you call this month, sometimes it's for the next year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then when they come to do the work, they'll say that you wasn't home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: They'll close the ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then you have to call the customer service number again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Half of the time, you're left to do your work on your own or just manage to live month to month just to make sure you can live decent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Sometimes you can't even get a hold of somebody to get a ticket order number because it's like you stay on the phone countless times and a long time at that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And you spend half of the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then when you do get a ticket, they tell you you have a ticket for that already.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And you have to then have it closed out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then you have to find a maintenance worker to close that ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then it leaves you back at square one with no work done and not even a work order ticket number.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Dickey, does that conclude your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: My thing was moving over.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Take your time.

chapters.summary: Dickey says the app glitches and sometimes does not provide a work order number, while staff later tell her the number no longer exists. She says tickets are closed unexpectedly and residents do not know when workers will come.
chapters.title: Dickey reports MyNYCHA app glitches and disappearing ticket numbers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Also, I would like to say there needs to be a better system because they say in the app, but when you go in there, it's like app glitches.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And sometimes you're not even able to like get the order number, the work order number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then when you go and try to read it, repeat the order number to them, they tell you that no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And it's like, it's really frustrating because you sit in here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And you don't know when somebody's going to come.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then when you're expecting somebody to come, next thing you know, the ticket is closed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: So my experience with work orders are very like half of the time I'm unsuccessful and I'm left just to manage without.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does that conclude your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Yes, I hope something can be fixed about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And like I said, I just really wish it was something better that we can do than to have tickets just keep piling up and no work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does that complete your testimony, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Dickey?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Miss Dickey?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Miss Dickey?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Yes, that's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: My Wi-Fi was doing a little in and out.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does that complete your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Please stay on because I have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Now we will move next to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Layla Glasgow.

chapters.summary: Layla Law-Gisiko identifies herself as Democratic District Leader for Chelsea and says she is testifying about Fulton Houses and Elliott-Chelsea Houses. She says buildings slated for demolition still need basic maintenance and that NYCHA and partners have failed to respond.
chapters.title: Layla Law-Gisiko raises Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea maintenance failures amid demolition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Chair, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: My name is Leila Logiziko, and I am the Democratic District Leader representing Chelsea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: And I'm here today to speak specifically about the conditions at Fulton Houses and Elio Chelsea Houses and about what appears to be an increasingly dangerous gap between NYCHA's obligations on paper and what residents are experiencing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: These buildings, as many of you know, are slated for demolition despite massive and continued opposition from tenants as well as the broader Chelsea community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: These buildings have not ceased to be people's homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: And yet, NITRA and its development partner-related properties have failed to provide adequate response to basic maintenance.

chapters.summary: Law-Gisiko says a tenant became locked in her apartment and the fire department had to break her door because NYCHA could not send a locksmith. She says the door remains unrepaired and a Fulton building entrance has been broken for weeks despite multiple tickets.
chapters.title: Law-Gisiko cites locked-in tenant and broken building entrance

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Let me give you a couple of examples.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Recently, a tenant became locked in her own apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Because Naisha was unable to send a locksmith to untrap the tenant, the fire department had to break her door to get her out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: The door has still not been repaired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: to this date.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: And she has now been told that the repair will take many weeks and maybe months because a carpenter is not available before at least two to three months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: That is putting her and her household at risk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: At Fulton Building 11, the front entrance door has been broken for weeks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Multiple tickets have been submitted, but repairs still await.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: These are not cosmetic issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: A functioning apartment door, functioning building entrance are among the most basic elements of safety and security in residential housing.

chapters.summary: Law-Gisiko says Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea are supposedly covered by a Meanwhile Plan that should add security, pest control, and repairs, but none of that is happening. She says residents are told their buildings are privatized while NYCHA still says it is the property manager.
chapters.title: Law-Gisiko says Meanwhile/Bridge Plan commitments unmet and NYCHA/PACT confusion

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: And these conditions are particularly troubling because Fulton and L.A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Chelsea are supposedly covered by a special interim program, the Meanwhile Plan, designed specifically to prevent this deterioration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: The master development agreement provides for a meanwhile or bridge plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: NITCHA's own public material described its purpose very clearly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: NITCHA would continue to manage the existing buildings until they were vacated, while the development partner, Related Properties, would add capacity to NITCHA management through additional security, pest control,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: building system repairs, and in-unit repairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: NITCHA later described the bridge plan as providing pest management, work ticket closeout, supplemental security, and support for heating and elevators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: None of this has happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: What residents are experiencing does not at all resemble this description.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Anecdotally, residents also report calling NITCHA for repairs and being

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: told in substance, your building has been privatized, we do not handle it anymore, by NYCHA respondents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: But NYCHA itself stated as recently as April that it remained the property manager for all Fulton and other Chelsea buildings and specifically instructed residents to continue submitting maintenance requests through NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: There should be no ambiguity for a tenant about who fixes a broken door.

chapters.summary: Law-Gisiko says residents who resist relocation find repair requests turn into relocation conversations and delays. She asks the Council to establish who is responsible for each repair category and whether residents slated for relocation receive the same maintenance service.
chapters.title: Law-Gisiko says repair requests become relocation pressure and lists asks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: There is another deeply troubling pattern.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Residents who have declined or resisted relocation report that when they submit repair requests, the conversation turns instead into relocation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: If I can have 30 more seconds, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Tenants are asked again to move, even though they have already said that they do not wish to move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: And their repairs are delayed even beyond what is the average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: I will just wrap it up by saying that, you know, residents routinely describe an extraordinary lack of timely response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Problems remain unresolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Calls are passed from one entity to the other.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Let me just skip all of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: So, okay, so here are the asks that I would like to place in front of the city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: I ask that the city council establish very concretely who is responsible today for every category of repair at Fulton and L.A.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: Chelsea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Layla Law-Gisiko
utterances.text: what services the Meanwhile or Bridge Plan is actually providing, building by building, how quickly work orders are being completed, and whether residents slated for relocation are receiving the same maintenance service as every other night shed tenant.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks Dickey about living without proper kitchen cabinets and relying on a temporary slop sink since September 9. Dickey says it is extremely hard because she goes to dialysis, cares for grandchildren, and can only use one arm.
chapters.title: Banks questions Patricia Dickey on living without kitchen cabinets

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions for the panelists, particularly Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Estrada and Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Dickey.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I'll actually start with Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Dickey, who resides in Pink Houses.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Dickey, since September 9th, you've been living without proper kitchen cabinets and relying on using a temporary slop sink, which I believe Knight gave to you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How has this setup impaired your ability to manage your household and take care of your family?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: It's extremely hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: First off, I have, like, I go to dialysis, so I need my function of my kitchen to work because I have to eat, like, eat in a certain way, and then I have grandchildren that's here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And it's like I'm using half of my kitchen, and then I can't lift stuff, and everything is all scattered, and they attend school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: So when I have my counter along with my sink, I was able to put things there because I can only use one of my arms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And it's like I'm left to just be moving halfway, like across my kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And it's really hard.

chapters.summary: Banks asks why NYCHA told Dickey remaining repairs would not be finished until March 2027. Dickey says she was told they were backed up, had no appointments, and that an outstanding paint order had to be closed first.
chapters.title: Banks asks Dickey about six-month repair timeline; she cites backlog and paint ticket

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And, you know, when NITRA staff told you that the remaining repairs wouldn't be finished until March of 2027, a six month wait.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What reason did they give you for that extreme timeline?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And did they claim they were backed up in any work orders or that they were waiting on skill trades?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: They was backed up and that they was also waiting, like, that there was actually no appointments available until then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And then reason being, like, we had a paint order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: I had a paint order before to put them to paint my whole house that was outstanding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: No long, how long I was waiting for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And they told me that was the reason of being holed up because I had to have that canceled out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: So that took an additional two weeks to close because everyone kept sending me around calling this one just for somebody to close out a ticket.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: So I can get the ticket in to match the work that needs to be done.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA ever assessed the safety or accessibility risks of leaving Dickey in an incomplete kitchen for six months. Dickey says no one from housing raised that concern until Banks's office intervened.
chapters.title: Banks asks Dickey whether NYCHA assessed safety risks; she says no

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And during their initial visit or any time before my office stepped in, did NITRA conduct any assessment on whether

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: living in an incomplete kitchen for six months posed safety or accessibility risks for you and your family?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: It was only like when you came in and stepped in, you understood my, like what I was thinking, like six months is a long time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Like you said, the holidays, as we chatted, the holidays is going to be coming up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And I enjoy you said just to sit down and eat as a family correctly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Like that's a huge part of my day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Like I want to hear what's going on with my grandkids and sit in my kitchen comfortably.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Like that's where we link up at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: And to sit down.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: But because my kitchen was so dismantled, even when you stepped in, you was like, you know, you can understand my housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: No one from housing ever said that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: It was just like, here's this sink and that should be fine.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how hard it was for Dickey to get clear updates from management before contacting his office. Dickey says it was very difficult and that work only started moving after the chair's office stepped in.
chapters.title: Banks asks Dickey about difficulty getting updates before intervention

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how difficult was it for you to get any clear updates or straightforward answers from the development management before you reached out?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: out to my office directly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: I can't believe even like the change that happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: I was almost like, wow, like I wish I would have reached out to you immediately when this happened because it took a whole lot off of me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
utterances.text: Like things started to move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Dickey
