chapters.summary: Daniel Greene identifies himself as NYCHA's Executive Vice President of Property Management Operations and introduces Heather Beck. He says safe and decent homes are at the heart of NYCHA's mission and thanks the committee for the opportunity.
chapters.title: Daniel Greene introduces NYCHA team and mission

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Chair Chris Banks, members of the Committee on Public Housing, other distinguished members of the City Council, NYCHA residents, community advocates, and members of the public.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm Daniel Green, NYCHA's Executive Vice President of Property Management Operations.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I am pleased to be joined by Heather Beck, Executive Vice President and Chief Real Estate Officer.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you for this opportunity to discuss our efforts to improve the repair process to better serve residents and enhance their quality of life.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Providing and maintaining safe and decent homes is at the heart of our mission, and everything we do is centered around our work to ensure that the authority remains a vital resource of affordable housing in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Today and for generations to come.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Despite the significant challenges of stewarding aging buildings that have long been underfunded by the federal government, we have made considerable progress these last several years

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: to become a better landlord, and we are pleased to share some of the details today.

chapters.summary: Greene says addressing significant capital needs is critical to reducing repairs and that Section 8 conversions through PACT and the Trust are primary tools. He says those programs renovate buildings and bring in partners for day-to-day operations.
chapters.title: Greene on capital needs and PACT/Trust as repair reduction tools

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In addition to the operational improvements we're implementing, we know that addressing the significant capital needs of our building

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: is critical to reduce the number of repairs needed, and Section 8 conversions through programs like PACT and the Trust are a primary tool to address capital needs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: These programs enable us to renovate buildings from top to bottom and bring in partners for their day-to-day operation.

chapters.summary: Greene says residents can submit repair requests through the Customer Contact Center or MyNYCHA app and website. A maintenance worker assesses and performs standard repairs, while complex work or lead/asbestos testing creates tickets for NYCHA staff or vendors.
chapters.title: Greene explains NYCHA work order process from request to skilled trades

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: First, I'd like to explain the work order process at NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Residents can submit repair requests by calling NYCHA's Customer Contact Center, or CCC, or by using the MyNYCHA app or website.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: A ticket is then created for a maintenance assessment in which a maintenance worker

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: assesses the repairs needed, and performs any standard repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: If complex repairs requiring skilled trades such as paint, plaster, carpentry, plumbing, or if lead or asbestos testing is needed, the maintenance worker will create tickets for NITRA staff or vendors to complete the repair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Residents can then call their neighborhood planner to schedule skilled trades appointments.

chapters.summary: Greene says the Neighborhood Planning Unit was part of NYCHA's 2021 Transformation Plan, developed in response to the 2019 HUD agreement. The plan focused on heat, elevators, pests, waste, lead, mold, and inspections.
chapters.title: Greene describes Neighborhood Planning Unit and Transformation Plan under HUD agreement

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The creation of the Neighborhood Planning Unit was one of the significant changes set forth in NYCHA's 2021 Transformation Plan,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: our vision for significant and sustainable change to NYCHA property management operations, as well as our overall organization.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Developed as part of NYCHA's response to the 2019 HUD agreement, the transformation plan established a strategic roadmap for addressing the authority's challenges, with a particular focus on the agreement pillar.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: areas of heat, elevators, pests and wastes, lead, mold, and inspections.

chapters.summary: Greene says the Neighborhood Model created smaller property management portfolios and new roles. Neighborhood planners and secretaries schedule skilled trades, service coordinators provide contacts, and contract managers review vendor work.
chapters.title: Greene details neighborhood roles and accountability

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Through the Transformation Plans Neighborhood Model, we created smaller property management portfolios that are easier to manage and feature increased accountability and resources.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And as I noted, we established several neighborhood-based roles to strengthen support for the properties and residents across key operational areas.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The neighborhood planner and the neighborhood secretary help schedule skilled trade work orders and improve coordination and communication with residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Neighborhood service coordinators provide residents with on-the-ground accessible points of contact, enhancing resident awareness of NITRA activities and initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And neighborhood contract managers review vendor work orders to ensure residents receive quality services from contractors.

chapters.summary: Greene says work order reform decentralized skilled trades and streamlined scheduling. Assigning trades to neighborhoods or developments reduces travel time and helps staff learn the unique needs of their sites.
chapters.title: Greene on work order reform and decentralized skilled trades

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Additionally, NYCHA aligns central office services with the new property management structure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: These reforms ensure that frontline leaders are supported and equipped to manage buildings effectively and deliver high-quality service to residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Work order reform, another key transformation plan initiative, decentralized skilled trades and streamlined the work order scheduling process, resulting in more efficient scheduling and completion of repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The programs assigned skilled trades to each neighborhood and to developments in some cases, in contrast to the previous borough assignments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: This eliminates delays due to travel times and allows skilled trade staff to become

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: better familiar with the unique needs of the developments they serve.

chapters.summary: Greene says residents now receive automated mail, email, or robocalls when work orders are created, scheduled, or upcoming. He says missed skilled-trade appointments fell to 2.7% in July 2026 from 10.9% two years earlier.
chapters.title: Greene reports automated communications and reduced missed appointments

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In addition to focusing on reducing wait times and repair backlogs, NYCHA is committed to improving the resident experience of the repairs process.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Residents now receive automated communication through mail, email, and or robocalls at key intervals for maintenance and skilled trades repairs, such as when a work order is created, scheduled, or upcoming.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Ensuring that appointments are not missed is central to improving the resident experience.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In partnership with the Federal Monitor, NYCHA has reduced its missed skilled trade appointments to only 2.7% of the 17,000 skilled trade appointments in July 2026, down from 10.9% two years ago.

chapters.summary: Greene says a 2025 survey found 78.6% of residents rated completed work orders as excellent or good in July 2026. He also describes pest management and TEMPO text-message pilots that increased appointment confirmations and coordinated relocations.
chapters.title: Greene cites resident satisfaction survey and text-message pilots

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In a resident satisfaction survey implemented in 2025 that surveys residents after every work order is completed, 78.6% of residents are reporting satisfaction rates of excellent or good in July of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: NICHA is using technology to better serve and communicate with residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For instance, the Pest Management Department launched a text messaging pilot in late 2023.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Residents who do not answer the phone to confirm appointments receive automated text reminders, resulting in an additional 2,400 appointments confirmations monthly.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: NICHA's landmark lead abatement program, TEMPO, also uses text messaging to coordinate hotel relocations with residents during the lead abatement process.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA partnered with the Federal Monitor to build dashboards tracking work order volume, backlog, production, service-level times, quality assurance, and missed appointments. He says these data-driven metrics guide maintenance performance.
chapters.title: Greene discusses performance dashboards and work order metrics

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Notably,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: ICHA partnered with the Federal Monitor and others to build comprehensive performance management dashboards that are updated regularly to track performance

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: in key metric areas, such as overall work order volume and backlog, work order production, service level times, quality assurance, and missed appointment tracking.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Our data-driven focus on performance results is also reflected in maintenance performance.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA maintenance workers receive about 98,000 new work orders per month and complete basic repairs in occupied apartments in less than four days on average. Since 2024, NYCHA has inspected every public housing apartment annually and created needed work orders.
chapters.title: Greene reports high workload, four-day basic repairs, annual inspections

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Of all trades, NITRA maintenance workers have the heaviest daily workload, receiving approximately 98,000 new work orders per month.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Despite the immense workload,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: NICHA is completing basic maintenance repairs in occupied apartments in less than four days on average with its on-site maintenance teams.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: At the same time, since 2024, NICHA has been inspecting all of its public housing apartments each and every year, completing basic repairs during the inspection and creating any additional work orders needed for skilled trade repairs.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA reduced the borough-based skilled trades backlog by 14% since 2024, down to 282,000 work orders. In 2025, NYCHA created 2.5 million repair work orders and closed or canceled about 2.49 million.
chapters.title: Greene reports skilled trades backlog down 14% to 282,000

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Despite apartment inspections increasing, the number of work orders created, we have reduced the borough-based skilled trades backlog by 14% since 2024, down to 282,000 work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: To put this backlog in perspective, during 2025 alone, 2.5 million new repair work orders were created and 2.49 million were closed or more in limited circumstances canceled.

chapters.summary: Greene says Maintenance Cares lets workers escalate high-need apartments directly to him and has resolved 1,164 apartments since February 2025. He says the FY2027 budget includes $20 million for the Critical Repairs Initiative to let residents escalate severe non-mold repairs.
chapters.title: Greene describes Maintenance Cares and Critical Repairs Initiative

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Despite these positive trends, some residents at NYCHA experience particularly challenging repair conditions due to the aging infrastructure and compounding.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: repair conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so NYCHA created new programs to address apartments with high repair needs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Maintenance Cares provides maintenance workers a means of escalating high-need apartments requiring critical repairs directly to me.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Since launching in February 2025, 1,164 apartments with major repair work needed have been resolved through the program, with over 100 apartments resolved in just the past 30 days alone.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In the fiscal year 2027 budget, the administration invested $20 million

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: in new expense funding to support NYCHA's Critical Repairs Initiative, or CRI, which will build off maintenance cares and enable residents to contact a call center to escalate repairs to address severe conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: CRI is an important component of the mayor's housing plan, inspired by the independent empathetic case management approach fostered through the Mold Ombudsperson Call Center, or OCC,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: an independent court-appointed entity that has worked with NYCHA case management staff to assist tens of thousands of residents with leak and mold complaints.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA has worked with the Mold Ombudsperson Call Center and independent analyst to prioritize mold and leak repairs. He says more than 69,500 mold inspections and related work orders closed by August 2026, and the Restore and Renew program aims to address 10,000 mold and leak work orders over two years.
chapters.title: Greene on mold/leak backlog progress and Restore and Renew

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Speaking of mold and leak complaints, our progress in tackling mold and leak work orders is another key example of the advances we're making.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Working closely with the OCC as an independent court-appointed data analyst, NYCHA has been able to better prioritize repairs and allocate limited personnel and financial resources.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Since our various backlog initiatives began in 2022 and 2023, more than 69,500 mold inspections and mold removal

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Mold-resistant paint, tub enclosures, and plumbing work orders have been closed as of August 2026 through specialized targeted efforts.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In 2025, we also rolled out the Mold and Leaks Restore and Renew program, aimed at adding more skilled trade resources and staffing to further reduce the backlog of skilled trade repairs needed as a result of mold and leaks.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration added an additional $10 million of support to the program over the next two fiscal years and is expected to help NYCH expand the program to more sites in the coming years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Approximately 4,000 work orders have been completed via the initiative so far.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It started last year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And the program's goal is to address 10,000 Mold and Leak work orders in total over the next two years.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA's average HUD INSPIRE score rose to 79.5 as of September 16, 2026, up from 32.5 in 2022 and 2023. He says 89% of developments passed inspections so far this year, up from 15% in 2022 and 2023.
chapters.title: Greene reports improved HUD INSPIRE scores and passing rates

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: NYCHA has made significant progress year over year to improve conditions in residents'apartments and buildings, a commitment reflected in the improvement in HUD physical inspection scores for NYCHA properties.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: HUD's new inspection standard, known as the National Standards for Physical Inspection of Real Estate, or INSPIRE, were unveiled in 2023 and implemented for NYCHA in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: As of September 16, 2026, I'm pleased to report that our average score has risen to 79.5, up from 32.5 in 2022 and 2023.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The number of developments that passed these inspections has also improved to 89% of developments passing so far this year, up from 15% in 2022 and 2023.

chapters.summary: Greene says NYCHA's Quality Assurance Unit improves performance and accountability for maintenance and repairs. He says the NYCHA website now publishes service outages, individual work orders, lead paint testing progress, and capital needs reports.
chapters.title: Greene on quality assurance and public transparency data

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In addition to our operational improvements, NYCHA has carried out several reforms to enhance transparency and accountability in recent years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: NYCHA's Quality Assurance Unit, developed in response to the HUD agreement, improves performance and accountability by ensuring that maintenance and repairs are completed to industry standards in alignment with our existing policies and procedures.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Additionally, NYCHA's website now features a range of publicly available data and information, service outages, individual work orders, and lead paint testing progress can all be tracked.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Reports are available with extensive information about our property's capital needs and our progress in meeting the various mandates of the HUD agreement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn things over to my colleague, Heather Beck, Executive Vice President and Chief Real Estate Officer, who will discuss work orders of the PAC developments.

chapters.summary: Heather Beck says investing in capital needs is key to reducing repairs and that PACT and the Trust generate billions in investment. She says comprehensive renovations and infrastructure upgrades will reduce building maintenance and repair needs.
chapters.title: Heather Beck on PACT capital investments and repair reduction

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you, Dan.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: As Dan stated, the key to reducing our need for repairs and enabling NYCHA to complete repairs as swiftly as possible is investing in our building's significant capital needs.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And that's why NYCHA is so focused on pursuing strategies that generate billions of dollars in investment for our portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Through massive infrastructure upgrades and comprehensive renovations, NYCHA's major housing preservation and stabilization programs, like PACT and the Trust, will reduce our building maintenance and repair needs.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: This will enable us to focus our resources where they are needed the most.

chapters.summary: Beck says PACT transitions day-to-day property management to private managers, but NYCHA oversees Section 8 administration, site visits, and compliance. She says NYCHA analyzes pest, mold, leak, elevator, and heat work orders monthly and reports that PAC work orders in those areas typically resolve within one day.
chapters.title: Beck describes NYCHA's oversight of PACT partners and monthly reporting

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: The PAC program transitions day-to-day responsibility of the property to new private property managers.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: However, NYCHA maintains an important oversight role of these properties in several key ways.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: NYCHA maintains administration of the Section 8 subsidy and ensures that PAC partners comply with specific Section 8 subsidy requirements, which includes inspections and waitlist policies.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We also conduct site visits to monitor PAC partner activities and respond to inquiries or issues.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: If performance gaps are identified, NYCHA works with the PAC partner to identify specific issues as they arise and agree on project solutions, and we monitor improvement and work on those plans.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We also analyze work orders for the categories including pests, mold, leaks, elevators, and heat on a monthly basis to ensure that they are being resolved in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Our monthly reporting indicates that work orders at PAC sites in these five areas are typically resolved within one day, and anyone can view that progress on our website.

chapters.summary: Beck says NYCHA launched an online PAC dashboard in 2023 showing quarterly maintenance, tenancy, and construction data. She acknowledges more work remains to reduce NYCHA's work order backlog and says NYCHA will keep collaborating with stakeholders.
chapters.title: Beck on PAC dashboard and remaining work

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: In 2023, NYCHA launched an online PAC dashboard that displays quarterly data on maintenance and repairs, tenancy proceedings, and construction progress.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Partners such as the Federal Monitor have acknowledged our progress.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Although we have made significant strides forward in our work to better serve all of our residents, yielding tangible results in terms of residents'living experience and the conditions of their homes, we acknowledge that there is still work to do

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: to further reduce NYCHA's work order backlog.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: With continued transformation as our guide, we will keep innovating and collaborating with all of our stakeholders to enhance our operations and delivery to residents to ensure that they have homes they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you for standing with us as we strive to improve residents'quality of life, and we appreciate your partnership and support.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We are here to answer any questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your statements, your opening statements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I guess we'll just dive straight into the questions.

utterances.text: And what are the total number of work orders open today in Section 9 and in PAC, respectively?

utterances.text: And what is the total number of work orders, including NITRA-wide, including Section 9, Section 8, and PAC?

utterances.text: And what would the estimated cost be to resolve this or the total?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for your question.

utterances.text: I'm just going to allow Ms.

utterances.text: Beck to give the PAC numbers before we get into that next question.

utterances.text: Again, so we collect work order data on the HUD key pillar areas.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that includes work order information on elevators, heat, leaks, mold, and pests.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that is a subset of the work orders that are created at each of our properties.

utterances.text: So the information I have for you is as of August 31st.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It's very likely that some of the work orders that were opened on the 31st have been resolved and closed, but I just want to make sure that that is clear.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So as of August 31st, there are 409 open work orders in the PAC portfolio among the 82,000 work orders that have been created over the past six years.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that's about one work order per 100 units.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And again, because our PAC partners are responding and closing or resolving work orders, typically within one day, we would expect most of those 409 work orders to be closed at this point in September.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And then the question that I posed just now.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So I want to note before I give this answer, on Section 8, NYCHA does not maintain records of open work orders within the Housing Choice Voucher Program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Apartment conditions are monitored through the regular annual housing quality standards inspection.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And as such, we're not able to estimate the total cost to resolve those work orders for Section 8.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For Section 9...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think the critical number here is our physical need assessment, which is the

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: which is the $78 billion, which will be reassessed in a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That really is the number to address comprehensively all the root causes and all the physical conditions necessary to address it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: On average right now, we're seeing 2.5 million work orders created.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: At NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So to put that backlog in perspective, we have 600 on the Section 9 side, we have 606,000 work orders as of today.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But every year, we're seeing 2.5 million work orders created.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And we're addressing about just over 2.4 million of them with some with some, you know, small number of cancellations in there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that level of effort, which we're at, by the way, the highest level of closing repairs that we have been, you know, in any recent year,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: really, we have to turn to our physical needs assessment because we need those comprehensive repairs in order to see that number really truly.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What was the most recent needs assessment done?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The most recent one, I believe it was done in 2022, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And published in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And published in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that is the $78 billion.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And it will be refreshed in, I think, five years from then.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, and that's handled by our asset and capital management.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they would be able to give you that schedule in more detail on the property management guy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But really, really.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The volume of work orders that we're experiencing right now is very high.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Because one thing I think it's important to note historically, before three, two years ago, we never inspected every apartment every year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So now we're inspecting 100% of our apartments every year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And when the maintenance worker goes in there, they're creating repair tickets because we're finding conditions that we probably have never found before.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're proactively going into apartments, creating the work orders and prioritizing them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Haven't we seen the number of work orders in Section 9 developments drop if units are moving to PAC?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And it's a very, very excellent question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I actually jumped, I unfortunately jumped the gun and got to get a little bit ahead of myself there.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I should have waited for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: You sure did.

utterances.text: So what really would change is how work orders are created.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So right now, again, we're inspecting about 140,000 apartments per year, give or take, to do those individual apartment assessments.

utterances.text: And when the maintenance worker does that, he or she are going to be generating more tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene

utterances.text: NYCHA was only in the past only doing 50% of those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And if we didn't get into that unit that year, it would be four years before the next inspection.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now we're...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Going in every single apartment every single year, and that's generating more work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're meeting our annual demand.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're doing...

utterances.text: Before let me ask this, I want to know what was the average time of completion for work orders in 2026, and based off of the priority level, including like emergency or non-emergency work orders?

utterances.text: And night to wide, how many work orders have been open this year for longer than six months, one year, two years?

utterances.text: So I have, thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.text: So overall, so 15% of the work orders that are open right now are between six months and a year.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me then move to this question.

utterances.text: And what is the breakdown for the total parent work orders and total child work orders?

chapters.summary: Banks notes skilled trade or vendor days-to-complete rose from 77 in FY2022 to 130 in FY2025. Greene says days-to-complete has come down this year, while the overall SLA metric includes aging open tickets such as paint and floor tile work.
chapters.title: Banks asks why trade completion times rose; Greene distinguishes days-to-complete from SLA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Days to complete, like the skilled trades or vendor work orders, increased from 77 in the fiscal year 2022 and to 130 in fiscal year 2025.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the days to complete, actually, the current year, the days to complete have come down for trades this year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: What has increased is the overall SLA for trades, which is, so there's two different metrics that we use to analyze time at NITRA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: First is the days to complete, and that will look at all the work orders that we closed in a given day or time period and how old those work orders were upon the date that they were completed.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that gives a good perspective of the work that we're getting done, where we're getting work done, how old is that work that we're getting done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The second metric that we use to measure time is the SLA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that's very important because that incorporates open tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the open tickets...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Age, and a lot of them are the, oh, that one year plus category, they age, and they're tickets that

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: mainly paint tickets, but also floor tile tickets and some other big chunks that age for a long time due to resource constraints and due to also some of the challenges logistically with doing some of that work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For example, floor tiles, where we have about 57,000 tickets open, those age because we need money for asbestos, which the city council has provided to us and the state has also provided to us, but without that funding

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: and also without relocation, we're not able to get that huge number done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But I can give you the days to complete as of today, which is illustrative of some of the improvements for the trades.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Council Member Elsie Encarnación asks how NYCHA defines a neighborhood under work order reform. Greene says NYCHA has 28 neighborhoods organized by geography, each generally about 5,000 units, with property managers reporting to a neighborhood administrator.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks how NYCHA defines neighborhoods; Greene describes 28 geographic portfolios

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Elsie Encarnacion.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I represent District 8, East Harlem and the South Bronx, the most concentration of nature developments in a district.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: In your opening statement,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: in regards to work order reform.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You talked about decentralizing the skill trades and assigning skill trades to each neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How do you define a neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So when the transformation plan took effect in 2022, 2023,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Nightshade was moved into about, currently now it's 28 neighborhoods, so it was originally 30.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've since gone down to 28.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's geography, really.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So geography, so for example, neighborhood five in Manhattan includes East River, Wagner, Jefferson, and Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So all neighborhoods in close proximity to one another, which reduces travel time amongst the trades.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that was the predominant factor.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Some neighborhoods, given where they are located, are a little bit larger than others.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But generally, we try to group things as geographically connected as possible.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are those the ones that you just named because they're all mine?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are they all in...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are they the only ones in that neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that is Neighborhood 5 in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I'll just use that as an example.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So Neighborhood 5 has a neighborhood administrator who oversees the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And then each of the four property managers at those properties report to the

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: the neighborhood administrator.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The neighborhood administrator also has, who reports to him, a neighborhood planner and a neighborhood planner secretary.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they are responsible for scheduling all of the skilled trade work for that neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Do they all have the same amount of developments per neighborhood?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Roughly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We try to have about 5,000 units altogether in each neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So each neighborhood has, some neighborhoods have three developments, some neighborhoods have five.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think our largest neighborhood is neighborhood four in Brooklyn, which is Hughes, Van Dyke, Brownsville, Woodson, Southwood.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Because everything is so close together.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, yeah.

utterances.text: We actually define simple repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Because when we do our 100% apartment inspections, we're actually required to go actually do the simple repairs when we do the inspection to convenience the residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're not creating follow-up tickets for the maintenance workers.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also do the five alive.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So when we go in there, we're going to check the CO alarms.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're going to check the fire safety sticker, the window guards, and some other safety-related items there to make sure that the apartment is safe.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And those are the core of the basic maintenance work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But every trade has certain, what we call at NYCHA, failure class problem codes in Maximo, in the system, of what they're assigned, what they're expected to do.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so maintenance workers have probably the largest number of those failure class problem codes that they're responsible for.

chapters.summary: Encarnación asks how many skilled-trade vacancies NYCHA has. Greene says there are 44 vacancies among 1,750 skilled trades, with plasters the hardest to hire, prompting a plaster academy, and about 30 maintenance vacancies.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks about skilled-trade vacancies; Greene reports 44 vacancies and plaster academy

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And how many job vacancies do you have in the skilled trades unit?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for asking.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So as of today, we only have 44 vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have 1,750 skilled trades.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And currently, as of today, we have 44, which is one of the lowest numbers that we've had for a while.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The highest trade that we have is plasters, which is about 14 vacancies as of today.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Plasters, we've talked about it at prior council hearings.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's a unique trade to NYCHA, the amount of plaster work that we have.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So going outside of NYCHA to find those individuals is difficult.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that's why we started a plaster academy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: On the maintenance side, I think we have about 30 vacancies as of today.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have 750 maintenance workers citywide and just 30.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're at very low vacancy rates overall.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And you have the budget if you had.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: A line of people outside that were ready to take on that job, you have the budget to pay those people and fill those vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yeah, we're pretty fast.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I mean, I think when I pulled the numbers in August, we had like 60 vacancies, and now it's down to 44.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's cyclical because we just also went through what they call a skilled trade pick, where trades are moved around the city based on seniority.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's a thing that we have with the unions contracted.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But, yeah, we're very low on vacancies, and that is also true for our caretakers, for janitorial staff as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're able to fill things very quickly for our HR department.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You're going to ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Encarnación asks who performs NYCHA's yearly apartment inspections. Greene says NYCHA maintenance staff do most, with a vendor used in the first years, and HUD INSPIRE inspectors provide outside annual review that can be skipped for high scores.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks who conducts annual inspections; Greene says NYCHA maintenance with HUD INSPIRE oversight

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know early in your conversation with the chair, you talked about the inspections that you have that you now do yearly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: These are done by NYCHA staff, the maintenance staff, you said?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Who does the inspections?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Predominantly NYCHA maintenance staff.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So there's a special work order, apartment inspection work order that they're trained to perform.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they're doing the vast majority.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We did bring in a vendor in the first couple of years because we were concerned.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We'd never had, before two years ago, we had never inspected every NYCHA apartment.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So it was kind of historic for us.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We brought in a vendor during the first couple of years to help us.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But right now we're really pretty self-sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also do have, it's a very, very difficult inspection regime by HUD.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: If we fail our Inspire inspection, we actually have to re-inspect all the units within 60 days.

chapters.summary: Encarnación says she doubts the high inspection pass rates given dilapidated apartments and the volume of work orders her staff handles. Greene says he is not declaring mission accomplished, visits developments daily, and points to Maintenance Cares and the Critical Repairs Initiative.
chapters.title: Encarnación challenges inspection pass rates against ground conditions; Greene cites Maintenance Cares and CRI

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: But you're inspecting yourselves and...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is there anyone outside of NYCHA who inspects yearly or?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: regularly any NITRA properties or NITRA units?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Councilman, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, that's the Inspire inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So those report to HUD REAC, which is a division of HUD.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And that's yearly?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They're yearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: If you get a certain score, they skip a year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So if you get above an 80, they'll skip one year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: If you get above a 90, they'll skip two years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And as I said, right now, approximately 87% have passed their 2026 Inspire inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I really attribute the passage rate to the apartment inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think it's been transformative because now we're getting into every unit.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And such as the conditions that were described by some of the panelists, which are very unfortunate, we don't want to have folks with missing cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We don't want to have folks with temp sinks.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So now they can escalate those repairs directly to prioritize them in our very lengthy scheduled process because we want those folks to go first.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We want to better prioritize.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So through the repairs of the apartment inspections, our really diligent work of our maintenance workers and prioritizing, I think we're starting to see a trend of better scores the past two years.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I think we're doing, we're about 120,000 inspections deep this year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we've already done 120,000, got about roughly 20,000 and a little bit less to go.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think we're going to come very close to hitting the actual 100% this year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think we're going to see this really be transformative for our residents.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'll be honest, I don't know how you're hitting those numbers, if I'm being extremely honest with.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: what I've been seeing on the ground in some of these apartments and knocking on some of these doors, it is extremely difficult for just all of our council staff.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Like a large number of our constituent services are essentially helping push these work orders.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I mean, if I look at my staff's notebooks, it's all work order numbers.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It's all of them following up, calling poor Brian, hearing from me every single day.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It is a lot of work that our offices are assisting with and helping with.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And a lot of it is in unit.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Issues that we're seeing in apartments.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And so I am very surprised that these inspections are going as well as they are.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I know that you guys are working hard, but it's a really big issue.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And a lot of these issues are just prevalent and really creating

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: an unsafe environment for the people that are living in these apartments.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It just is.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I mean, we see it day in and day out, especially with the amount of nitrous that we have in our development.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It's really, really difficult to believe that we would have this high of a percentage of

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: passing inspection rates for these dilapidated, in many cases, apartments.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I just have to be on record saying that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I just want to just be clear.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm by no means a mission accomplished person.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm at a development every day except for today because I'm here because I want to see the conditions on the ground, what the residents are experiencing, what our staff are experiencing.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And it's extremely tough conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I visit apartments every week and there are unacceptable conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: What we're trying to do, though, is proactively identify those uninhabitable conditions and connect those resources with our trades, with our resources to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's why we started Maintenance Cares.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So any maintenance worker in the city can email me and my team so that we can prioritize apartments like you see and your staff see every day.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We don't want folks living in those conditions, and then we try to work with residents to address that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The other thing that we're really excited about is the critical repairs initiative, which is going to allow residents through a formalized process to escalate non-mold and leak repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They can already escalate mold and leak through the OCC, but now missing cabinets, temporary sinks, damaged floors.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Through the CRI program, residents are going to be able to leverage off of that and come into us, and we have some additional money as well to support us on the overtime, which is critical for doing many of these jobs as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're very appreciative to the administration for supporting the CRI program, and we think it's going to be also transformative to, again, push those repairs because we don't want folks living in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We want to find them and correct them.

chapters.summary: Encarnación says it should not be residents' or council staff's job to constantly follow up on NYCHA work orders. Greene responds that he understands and thanks her.
chapters.title: Encarnación says residents and council staff should not chase work orders; Greene acknowledges

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm just saying that it's not our staff's responsibility or job to

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: to be continuously following up on NYCHA work orders.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It's also not really the residents.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Like these things should be working seamlessly.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You guys should be wanting, property managers should have access to work orders from the planning unit, understanding, calling, and reaching out.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: That is part of the job of property management, right?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: We are not and should not be the ones, and neither should that be falling on residents'backs to be constantly calling and following up and figuring out where their work orders are, when a person's coming, if they came missing work.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: It is extremely intensive on the residents, on our staff, in order to do this.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And I think that there has to be a more fluid method for you guys to be actively going out and following up on these work orders and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, counselor.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We are also joined by Councilmember Osei, who has joined us via Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how Maximo specifies response times and maintenance follow-up for emergency and non-emergency work orders. Greene describes nine priority levels, from one-hour priority nine super hazards to routine priority three work orders, and says superintendents monitor Maximo daily.
chapters.title: Banks questions Greene on Maximo priority levels and response times

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I guess I'm going to move forward with my line of questions, back to my line of questions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Understanding Maximo.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How do work orders typically specify response times for repairs in the Maximo system, including for emergency and non-emergency work orders?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And also, too, how does the Maximo represent the required practices for maintenance worker to follow up on specific repairs?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, and I should say thank you, Chair, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have nine priority levels for work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I'll start with the highest priority and I'll move down the group.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we first have what we call a priority nine work order, which is defined as a quote unquote super hazard work order.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: An example could be an elevator out of order with a passenger stuck or a gas leak.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so the response time for priority nines should be within one hour is what we're going to target for under our procedure manual.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For hazard, for the next classes would be a class eight or a hazard, which are really pretty rare class work orders that are priority eight.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're talking about sidewalk shed violations or rubbish violations by the Department of Sanitation.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The next category is very important, which is priority seven, which is a 24-hour response period.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And this is deemed a critical work order, but we basically on a day-to-day just define it as an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The key thing for priority seven is this leak from above.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So leak work orders would be priority sevens, stoppages, priority sevens, CO detectors that are not working, exit signs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: in those, but the biggest one that, you know, that we focus really intensively on is the leaks in the similar flooding condition work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Priority six is really reserved.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The predominant one is mold and mildew.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that was kind of a category that was used under the bias case.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So mold and leaks is priority six work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Priority five is stoves.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Again, not really seen that much.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The other big category I'll just skip to it is priority three, which is the routine work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So painting, you know, non-emergency type repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So Maximo prioritizes every work order.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The dashboard that I actually have up right now in Maximo, you can refresh it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Any minute and it will pull up any new ticket that has been created under those priority codes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Our superintendents and assistant superintendents, one of their primary jobs is to monitor Maximo throughout the day to see what tickets are coming in and then assign them to the maintenance workers based on their priority.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So when the maintenance...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to supervision, obligations from supervision, Representative Maximo, how are the supervisory inspections of work orders logged?

chapters.summary: Banks asks how supervisory inspections of work orders are logged in Maximo. Greene says they use IN inspection tickets and that completion of skilled-trade supervisory inspections has risen from the low 40s-50s to high 70s-80s percent.
chapters.title: Banks asks how supervisory inspections are logged; Greene describes IN tickets and improved completion

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the supervisory inspections are logged through Maximo.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's a different.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's an inspection ticket called an IN ticket.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so we've done a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: There's different types of inspections depending on different types of work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Over the past couple of years, we worked the monitor to greatly increase the completion of skilled trade supervisory inspection work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It was low 40s, 50s.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now we're up in the high 70s, 80s percents for completing the supervisory inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that's actually completing the inspection, going into the apartment and attempting it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: On the maintenance side, we do have follow-up work orders for mold and leaks.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do quality insurance inspection as part of the bias procedure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that applies to a large group of work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're actually rolling out a new inspection work order for maintenance workers for the apartment inspections.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the superintendent will get a certain number of work orders.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The superintendent will actually get a work order assigned to them through Maximo on their handheld and they'll have to go out and check apartment inspections that were done by the maintenance worker to make sure they're being done properly.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how notices to residents are logged in Maximo. Greene says Maximo has a communication log, notices are auto-printed or emailed before skilled-trade appointments, and calls to residents are logged through the linked Siebel system.
chapters.title: Banks asks how resident notices are logged in Maximo; Greene describes communication log and auto notices

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, and when it comes to notification protocols, Representative Maximo, how are notices to residents logged?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So Maximo does have a communication log function in it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So notices should be given in advance of the work order.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They're auto printed and delivered to the resident, in some cases emailed and mailed to the resident, especially in advance of skilled trade appointments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: These tickets, our turnaround time is so fast that we're really coming, you know, we're really contacting the resident and letting them know that we're coming or we're, you know, we're coming when right soon after the ticket was created.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But also in Maximo, we are able to call the resident if they have an updated phone number in the Siebel system.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Maximo links to Siebel.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we can actually call the resident and that logs into the communication log of Maximo.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we can make sure that that's a big issue.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So missed appointments has been a big focus for us on skill trades.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how NYCHA uses Maximo data to assess nonconformance, vendor issues, performance indicators, and asset needs. Greene says staff review Maximo daily, vendor data management needs improvement, and Maximo is used for lead abatement and building line leak prioritization.
chapters.title: Banks asks how Maximo data is used for nonconformance, vendors, and asset trends

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how does NITRA use the data from Maximo to assess work orders for nonconformance?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I mean, we look at my staff and I, we review Maximo every single day, minute, you know, from my position down to the borough VPs, to the skilled trade directors, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to vendors, how does NITRA use the data information for Maximo to assess the vendor?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Vendor issues.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's still an area that we need to, I think, develop more and work on.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're working with the monitor on a better vendor management protocol.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do have a statement of services that has to be signed by our superintendents and overseen by our neighborhood contract managers, which arose a couple years ago from the scandal that we had with DOI recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But data is definitely something that we could leverage more on the vendor side, which I just want to note, vendor is predominantly, in my world, paint and tile.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's the vast majority of it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how does NITRA?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the performance indicators, does NITRA get it from the work orders?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And has Maximo improved such that NITRA can determine work order, the work order trend or asset needs based on work orders in the system?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do use it for those assessments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In my world, on the property management healthy home side, we use it definitely heavily for lead abatement planning and protocols.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also use it for the building line initiative protocols to identify lines that have high numbers of leak work orders to prioritize them for repair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to work order closure without repair, in

chapters.summary: Banks asks what controls NYCHA added after DOI found falsified safety checks following the Butler House fire. Greene says Maximo now has photo requirements, labor logs, quality assurance, compliance, and environmental health teams, and lead abatement closures require uploaded reports and verification.
chapters.title: Banks asks about controls after DOI falsification findings; Greene cites photos, labor logs, and audits

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 2016, after the Butler House fire, DOI inspected 240 apartments and five developments to check whether the maintenance staff were inspecting and reporting safety items on work orders.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And they found that a staff had falsified documents claiming to have performed safety checks they had not performed.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What controls did NYCHA put in place after the report to confirm that and what worker enters a work order that matches the condition of the apartment?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's a report predates my time a little bit, NITRA, but I can talk about the HUD agreement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I was the chief compliance officer for NITRA for the first few years of the HUD agreement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've put in numerous controls in Maximo to prevent deceptive practices, including photograph requirements, labor logs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In addition, we have a quality assurance team, a compliance team, and environmental health and safety team that also follow up on work orders to check on conditions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And if any malfeasance is found.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is timestamp also used?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Everything is addressed in Maximo as far as I understand that term.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Location verification as well?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Location, yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, each work order is somewhat different on location.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, location, everything is tied to an apartment string, a room in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how many closed work orders did NITRA audit?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By physical inspection in 2025, and what share were found to be inaccurately reported?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I don't have that number for 2025, but I do have that number for the first quarter of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You can get us those numbers and then...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You can give us another 2026.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So 2026, if I recall correctly, it's in my notes, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: About 3,500 inspections were done, QH inspections were done, and about...

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: About 3% were found to be unsatisfactory.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that would then require a follow-up by the property to address the condition.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And in December of 2020, the DOI report reported 163

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: letter abatement work orders with false signatures of an EPA certified supervisor and said it had believed that the

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: True number was much higher.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can a work order in Maximo be signed or closed under a supervisor's credential or by someone other than that supervisor?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair, for your question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I am familiar with that, and much of my time at NYCHA has been building the lead paint abatement program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the inspections that you're referring to, I believe, in DOI were things that were submitted to HPD for apartment exemptions, the HPD apartment exemption process.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They weren't really associated with Maximo.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: What we have done in Maximo, though, is for lead abatement, we now have strict closure requirements.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So all of the required reports must be uploaded by the NITRA staff and the vendor and verified before they can be closed out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also are audited every six months on lead abatement by our environmental health and safety, and we're under the federal HUD agreement, which allows the monitor full access to our lead abatement files.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many employees NYCHA disciplined or terminated for falsifying work orders since 2020 and how many referrals were made to DOI or the Inspector General. Greene says he does not have that data broken down and that some information would come from DOI.
chapters.title: Banks asks about discipline and referrals for falsified work orders; Greene lacks data

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Since 2020, how many employees has NITRA disciplined or terminated for falsifying work order entry?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Chair, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I don't have that data broken down by year, but that would be something we'd have to follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many referrals has NYCHA made to DOIs, Inspector General for NYCHA, for suspected work order falsification since 2020?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how many were substantiated?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I don't have the answer, and some of that would have to come from DOI, but I will say that we work with...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many complaints of falsified or improperly closed work orders did NYCHA receive from residents in fiscal year 2025, and how many of those were investigated?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I don't have that number today, but our compliance department and DOI can provide those numbers.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether PAC partners must report suspected work order falsification to NYCHA or DOI. Heather Beck says PAC partners report monthly on HUD pillar work orders, but NYCHA does not collect or receive reports on falsification.
chapters.title: Banks asks if PAC partners must report suspected work order falsification; Beck says no

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Do PAC partners have any obligations to report suspected work order falsification to NYCHA or DOI?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Beck to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So PAC partners are reporting to us on that monthly basis in those different pillar areas.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Again, we are tracking work order resolution through that reporting process.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many such reports have you received?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We receive a report from every team every month of the year.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many reports have you received?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So we started collecting reports for the projects that had been closed starting in January of 2021.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Have you received any reports on 4?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Falsification?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: No, we don't receive or collect reports on falsification.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: From the RADPAC?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Got you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about Operation Mold Cleanup and tickets closed by contacting residents. Greene says a separate verification program reached 11,000 residents and closed about 3,000 tickets under an independent analyst, while Operation Mold Cleanup addressed about 35,829 tickets, with 678,752 mold and leak work orders closed since 2022.
chapters.title: Banks asks about Operation Mold Cleanup; Greene explains 35,829 tickets closed and stricter closure rules

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In 2022, NITRA launched what we call the Operation Mold Cleanup to close out mold and leak tickets left from the COVID period.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By contacting residents by email and phone, how many tickets were closed that way?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, uh,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Not just by, that's not Operation MOLC.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's not the full definition of Operation MOLC cleanup.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we do have a program verification program that we do with our independent data analyst, which is a court-appointed analyst by a federal court.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So in that program, which is a different program, we've reached out to 11,000 residents, and they verified approximately a third of the work is no longer needed.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so those, I think it's roughly around 3,000, those tickets were closed with the oversight of that independent data analyst, which is, again, reports to the federal court.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
