utterances.text: Another approximately 7,000, 8,000 were still required, work was still needed, and so those would be scheduled.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Operation Mold Cleanup was an effort that we looked at backlog cleaning tickets and tub enclosure tickets that we needed to address that were aging and were contributing to significantly poor conditions in units.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So through that effort, which continues today, we addressed over 30.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: about 35,829 tickets through Operation Mold Cleanup, which is a program to expedite and prioritize certain mold work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Overall, since 2022, we've closed out 678,752 mold and leak work orders.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the monitor's first report in 2019 found tickets closed with the repair being made and closure rules changed after that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is today's open work order count a true picture of the conditions that then the count in 2019?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's an excellent question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think things have dramatically changed since 2019.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The closure rules, especially around leak and mold, are some of the strictest closure rules, if not the strictest at NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They cannot be closed unless we physically get into the apartment and verify the work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That was why that 11,000 pilot program that we did with our.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Independent data analyst was so important because it was overseen carefully and was trying to look at some of these older tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Because sometimes folks get frustrated when we show up to verify and have to get into the apartments to verify like a paint ticket.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: A significant portion of the open mold only tickets are for painting.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And we want to, you know, we have to get in there and verify them.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the rules have dramatically changed, which makes it harder to bring the backlog down because to actually get in, we have to get, you know, to actually close the work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have to get in there and verify it, which is a good thing, too.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Definitely not complaining.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Definitely something that keeps us aggressively trying to work and get into folks'apartments to see if the work is needed.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA publishes work order closures without repair separately and who outside NYCHA checks closed tickets. Greene says he is unsure if that data is published but NYCHA shared 7.5 million work order transactions with the Council, and outside checks include the monitor, DOI, compliance teams, and independent analysts.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA publishes closures without repair and who checks closed tickets

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NYCHA publish work order closures without repair separately from repairs made?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I don't know if we do.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We could.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We could.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I have that data and happy to share it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We could.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: In 2026, this is not the full picture, but...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, why is it not published?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I don't know if it is or isn't.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Honestly, I don't know if it's published, but it certainly is data that we have.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And we have provided, I do want to note, to the Oversight and Investigation Division of the Council, we provided about 7.5 million work order transactions

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: and all of the underlying data to the OID at the City Council to begin to understand some of the closure requirements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And besides the monitor, who outside of NYCHA checks whether a closed ticket was repaired in Section 9 or on the PAC sites?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So on the Section 9 side, it would be the Federal Monitor, DOI, and then the three compliance departments developed and created by the HUD agreement.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And on the PAC side, who inspects where the ticket is?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So under the PACT program, we are under the same requirements for the, most of the same requirements for BIAS.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So for mold and leak work orders that are reported to NYCHA, those are then shared with an independent mold analyst and the independent data analyst.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And the independent mold analyst will go out to inspect closed leak and mold work orders on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And they're required to...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The independent analyst comes from...

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It's a court-appointed independent analyst.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And those are done on completed work orders, and they have to complete a statistically significant number of apartments each month.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many 311 complaints NYCHA received under Local Law 127 in FY2025 and what happens when a PAC tenant calls 311 about a water leak. Greene says NYCHA does not track routed 311 calls, while Beck says an inspector reviews conditions and violations require PAC partners to open work orders.
chapters.title: Banks asks about Local Law 127 311 complaints and PAC 311 leaks

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to getting an inspection, pursuant to local law 127,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: of 2021, 3-in-1 must take NITRE repair complaints.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many 3-in-1 calls or complaints were sent to NITRE in fiscal year 2025, and how many became work orders?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So NYCHA does not track the number of calls to the CCC that were routed through.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: through on one, they would treat them like another call and they would create a work order based on the...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I do want to, IMA, the independent mold analyst also is another inspector at Section 9 Developments and they've been inspecting us for, you know, numerous years.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to PAC sites, if a tenant finds a property manager to be unresponsive,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: and calls 311 about a water leak, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yeah, so residents, all of our residents at PACT properties have the ability to call 311 to request an inspection.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: To my knowledge, an inspector would come out and review the conditions.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: If a violation is issued, the PACT partner is required to open a work order for that.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And we will collect that information in our monthly reporting.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: That information is then independently verified by the independent mold analyst.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And I just say, in addition to 311, residents at PAC sites can also call NYCHA and request a separate HQS inspection if they're having issues with work order resolution.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether HPD inspects NYCHA tenant 311 water leaks and how tenants get HPD inspections. Greene says HPD refers NYCHA cases to NYCHA, HPD inspects court cases, and a new state law now gives NYCHA daily HPD inspection data that creates work orders.
chapters.title: Banks asks about HPD inspections and court repairs for NYCHA tenants

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And if a NYCHA tenant calls during one about a water leak, does HPD come out?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: No, HPD would refer to NYCHA to investigate.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how would a NYCHA tenant get an HPD inspection?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: HPD, I'm sorry, I didn't mean to speak over you.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So HPD inspects cases that come through the court.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the HPD, a judge assigned to an HPD.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can an HPD action bring forth a...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A response.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so actually under a new state law, um, HPD is, uh, is giving NYCHA a data download of its inspections of NYCHA every, every day.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now, before we used to only get paper records, um, and have to manually enter it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that was just up until last summer.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We now get a daily download, um, and that creates the work orders, uh, or creates basically a work order off of the HPD inspection.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And once HPD inspects and writes a violation, does NYCHA make the repair or does the tenant have to go back to housing court?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Well, we should be making the repair in accordance with the stipulation in housing court.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have a court order repairs procedure of how to handle those HPD generated repairs that we basically have to work with the resident on access dates or if the resident so stipulates how the access dates put forth in the stipulation.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for FY2022-2025 data on housing court cases, HPD violations, and corrected violations. Greene provides partial September 2025-present data: 551 HP cases, 5,312 violations, and about 31% closed, and says he was not involved in the lawsuit that led to transparency.
chapters.title: Banks requests housing court data and asks why lawsuit was needed for transparency

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you provide data for FY 2022, FY 23, 24, and 25 on

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: housing court cases initiated by NYCHA tenants to address unresolved maintenance conditions, including the number of HPD violations associated with those cases?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The number of violations that were corrected by NYCHA after the court filing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And three, the number of violations that remained unresolved until a court order, stipulation, or the housing court intervention was issued.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I have part of that data today for the past year.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We'll have to follow up on the early years, but I can give you the data from September 2025 to present.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you can.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Do you want to give you a for?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You have 25, right?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yeah, I have 25.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have, there were 551 orders to show causes commencing an HP case received by our law department.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Of that, out of those cases, there were 5,312 total violations received.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That also, that could actually include a little broader because some violations might come through non-payment cases where a court might also order an HPD inspection in a non-payment case if there's a cross-claim for open repair tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, and then roughly about 31% of the violations have been closed based on our work order system records.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And we're still working.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: This is a new process.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It just came about.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're still working with HPD.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that number is subject to change, but that's where we're at today.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, we now know that violations from those inspections basically only started showing up in HPD.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Our line was released since October of 2025.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But after the settlement with the New York lag, why did it take the lawsuit to become transparent?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that lawsuit, so I can't speak to its outcome.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But I will say that we strive to be transparent on these matters and more transparent.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So a lot of the issue might be data.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now we have much better data.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: As I said, just last year we were getting paper copies of these reports, which are obviously not sufficient to properly track.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA would allow HPD to inspect closed tickets quarterly and why NYCHA should be the only landlord that inspects itself. Greene says NYCHA is willing to discuss outside inspections and cites HUD, the Federal Monitor, and independent mold analysts, and says he will take back the idea of inspecting 311 complaints.
chapters.title: Banks presses on HPD inspecting closed tickets, NYCHA self-inspection, and 311 inspections

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Would NYCHA object to HPD inspecting a sample of closed tickets each quarter and publishing them?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Publishing what it finds?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're willing to work and talk about anybody to come and check out our buildings.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We want our residents to be safe, and we want to make sure that we're transparent.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Given NYCHA's history, why should it be the only landlord in the city that inspects itself?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I would just say I can't answer that from a policy perspective, but what I will say is we don't only just inspect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do have HUD inspections that are from outside entities.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also do have the Federal Monitor and the Independent Mold Analysts and other outside entities inspecting.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, NIT should be open to inspecting apartments in response to 311 complaints and reporting what it finds.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Definitely something I'll take back and speak to the NITRO leadership about.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Has NITRO had any conversations with HPD about creating a process that gets a tenant an inspection and a repair without having to make two trips to housing court?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I am not familiar with any communications, but I know that we've been talking with HPD a lot about this new daily data upfeed and this new process that we're engaged in.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what NYCHA considers a manageable number of open work orders. Greene says he cannot give a number, notes NYCHA receives about 2.5 million work orders per year, and says the agency is meeting annual demand.
chapters.title: Banks asks what NYCHA considers a manageable open work order count; Greene cannot give a number

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to targets for work orders, open work orders,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What does NYCHA consider a manageable number of open work orders?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And, yeah, you can answer that question first.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: What do I consider?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What does NITRA consider as a manageable number for open work orders?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Interesting question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think right now we are meeting our annual demand.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: of the work orders that are coming in.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Obviously, we also have some new initiatives that I'm very happy about, particularly the MLRR program that allowed me to hire 47 new trades to target mold and leak work orders over 100 days.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm also very happy with having programs such as CRI and maintenance cares to prioritize critical repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I can't give you a number.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Obviously, we want the work orders to be as low as possible.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But when you're receiving 200,000 work orders per month, 2.5 million work orders per year, that's the number that we have to manage.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's the number that I'm asked to manage.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so that's what we're going to continue to do to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many developments operate under work order reform and how repair times compare. Greene says all properties use the neighborhood planner model, with 28 planners and 28 neighborhoods, and that missed trade appointments have dropped to 2.7%.
chapters.title: Banks asks about work order reform and multi-trade scheduling; Greene says all neighborhoods use model

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, work order reform was launched in 2022 to allow residents to schedule.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Excuse me, multi-trade repairs to neighborhood planners more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Under the old system, residents were prevented from scheduling the next step in the repair process until the previous step was completed.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Developments are operating under these reforms today and how were the day to complete repairs and those developments affected

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: compared to other developments not operating under these reforms?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: All of our properties are operating.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: under the neighborhood planner model.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have 28 neighborhood planners assigned to the 28 neighborhoods with the same protocols and same resources.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Repair times for our trades have improved and missed appointments have significantly dropped.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So again, we're about 17,000, 18,000 appointments per month for the trades.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And right now, missed appointments is down to our lowest level.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I caution to say ever at 2.7%.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're only missing less than 500 appointments per month out of the 17,000 scheduled appointments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: A lot of the work is also being completed early.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do give long repair times because we only have a certain number of trades and a certain number of hours in a day.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Then we do have an overtime budget as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But we have to sequence things in accordance with how long a job takes.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Each job has a job plan and we have to schedule things in accordance.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So plaster, for example, could be a multi-day job.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have 37,000 open plaster tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We can't schedule them all next week because we just don't have enough plasters.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have 245 plaster teams, I believe, around that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So it's insane.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about normal wait times for trade repairs and what an ideal time would be. Greene says the current average scheduling window is about seven months, while three to four months would be more ideal, though prioritization and overtime are used for urgent repairs.
chapters.title: Banks asks normal and ideal wait times; Greene says about seven months now, three to four months ideal

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So what's the normal wait time?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So right now, I looked at this, about seven months on average right now.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That's how far we're scheduled out.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But what we do every day is sometimes folks are not available for their appointments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So if, for example, a carpenter shows up and a resident is not ready, if they say I am ill or whatever, that carpenter doesn't just go sit on his hands for the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: He goes and tries to find another job.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the average is seven months wait time.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So in an ideal situation, how long would it take to get to?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: attend it?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Obviously, I'd like to get those repairs done as soon as possible, you know, three, four months, you know, would be, obviously, everybody wants their repairs done tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I'm sure that when I say three, four months, folks are going to say, you know, that might not be reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But what we also try to do is, is look at prioritization factors.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So is it something, is this an urgent repair that we have to get done, push to the top of the priority schedule or use overtime to address?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We also do like in a situation like Miss Dickey or Miss Estrada.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Where they put in a ticket and they waited.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: They got a date of maybe seven months out to actually have a completion of their kitchen.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Would you say that is acceptable?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It doesn't sound acceptable, but it's the reality of where we are with the repairs that we have today and the number of trades and staff that we have.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have 81,000 carpenter tickets, so we have to come up with a fair way to prioritize those resources in a systemic way.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Every day we're scheduling out our carpenters.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Every day our carpenter backlog has actually come down by about 4,000 tickets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've also changed the way that we're ordering cabinets so folks are not waiting for cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have a bevy of cabinets.

chapters.summary: Banks says residents are not experiencing NYCHA's reported responsiveness, citing Dickey and Estrada's cases, and asks if the system is broken. Greene respectfully disagrees, says NYCHA completes much work and sometimes early, and points to the Critical Repairs Initiative for missing cabinets and temporary sinks.
chapters.title: Banks challenges NYCHA's numbers against on-the-ground cases; Greene disputes that system is broken

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It's easy to throw numbers out, but on the ground, this is not happening.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Folks are not.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, seeing, they're not actualizing these numbers that you're throwing out and quote unquote the responsiveness of NITRA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You saw this in these two early on in the pre-panel

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: that had we not interceded, these residents would have been waiting one seven months and the other one close to two months.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So, I mean, listen, you did say this is the reality.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the reality that the system is broken and it doesn't work?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: No, that's...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You don't have to agree on the record.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: No, I'm going to respectfully disagree.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We are getting, again, a lot of work done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And there are unfortunate cases, but we also are completing work early.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: early in a lot of the instances.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have to give folks a scheduled date.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We cannot bump appointments because that's bumping somebody else's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we want to make sure that we are being fair and equitable in distributing appointments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And one thing I will note, one thing I do want to know on the record is that

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Through the CRI program that we're trying to create, missing cabinets and holes in the walls and temp sinks is one of the items that we're going to be looking forward to pushing faster.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what "pushing faster" means under the Critical Repairs Initiative. Greene says CRI includes overtime funding, materials costs, and prioritization of items like missing cabinets, holes in walls, and temporary sinks.
chapters.title: Banks asks how CRI will speed repairs; Greene explains overtime, materials, and prioritization

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So when you say pushing faster.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Walk me through how that looks.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the way that it works is we do have, number one, we were allocated certain money for overtime under CRI.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The work has to be funded.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The trades don't work for free.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The capitalists cost money.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We spend $22 million a year in carpentry material at NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So faster means how long would it take, let's say, a ticket is put in, a work order is put in to get the work completed?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So you used to go faster, so I want to know what faster.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It's faster two months, three months, seven months, eight months?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're talking about carpentry or we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It could be carpentry.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So carpentry, to get that faster, you know, number one, what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you want to break it down, you can do carpentry.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You can break it down by whatever the work order is.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What does faster look like?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're not going to be able to cut it to 30 days.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Right now, we have, let me just pull up my numbers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You can cut it below seven months.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you cut it below seven months?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So one thing we have to go back to is our P&A, which is the overall physical needs for the property.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Then we have to look at the staffing and the number of work orders.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether hiring 565 workers today could reduce the backlog to 200,000 within a year, noting a similar 2013-2014 reduction. Greene calls it theoretical, says NYCHA is focused on doing and verifying work rather than closing tickets to lower numbers, and cites the MLR program.
chapters.title: Banks asks hypothetical 565-worker hire and 2013 backlog drop; Greene cites quality concerns

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: On January 2013, NYCHA had approximately 423,000 open work orders.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: To address the backlog, NYCHA hired 565 additional employees and assigned them to repair work.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: By January of 2014, the number of open work orders had reportedly fallen to approximately 106,000.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Although there were some reports that raised concerns that some of this reduction may have resulted from work orders being closed without repairs being completed,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: the reported decline was still unsubstantial.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If NITRA was provided with sufficient resources to hire 565 workers today, could it reduce the current work order backlog to 200,000 open work orders within a year?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I think that's all theoretical, which is fine sitting in this room here today.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But number one, one point that you made that was very important from your own report was there was a lot of concerns about the quality of that work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: One of the things that we've tried to change is not allowing staff to just close out tickets just to get the backlog down, just to look good in a press release to say that we got the backlog down.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We want to make sure that we're actually doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're closing out more than 70% with labor for our repairs right now for the trades.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we want to make sure the work is done and verified.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Just closing out tickets based on loose work order rules is not the way to get NYCHA better.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It just simply is not.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We have added trades where that is reasonable and where we have actually have funding to tie to it in a program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The key one that we added is the MLR, 47 trades directed and managed by the Office of Mold Assessment and Remediation to address aging mold and leak workers over 100 days.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've knocked down work orders at Whitman.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've knocked down work orders at Ingersoll, Red Hook East.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now we're working at Baruch, Wagner, Jefferson.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we're using data to target those sites with our monitor, with the IMA.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have done those initiatives, but everything has to be scaled and reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And the city's been very generous in providing resources, not only for that program, but also now over time for CRI as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We know there was a drastic reduction.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: between 2013 and 2014, sorry, from the 2013 and 2014 result,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: at least in part from the underreporting or the premature closure of repairs requests.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Was that drastic reduction because of underreporting or the premature closure of repair requests?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I cannot speak to that because I didn't work at NYCHA back then.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I came in 2019 as the chief compliance officer, and the reason why I was hired at NYCHA was because of efforts to close out work orders without doing proper work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And we've tried to change that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And part of the way we've changed that is by strengthening the work order closure rules and by increasing how work orders get created, most notably through the apartment inspections, most notably through how we work on lead and mold tickets so they have to be created.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, again, I would not want to get into a program where I'm only trying to produce the work order numbers so the numbers look better.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm here to address NYCHA as it stands with this $78 billion P&A.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what headcount by trade would maintain the backlog and what it would cost to reduce it to 200,000 over five years. Greene says 1,700 skilled trades currently maintain the backlog and will follow up, while noting work orders require physical work and resident relocation for asbestos.
chapters.title: Banks asks headcount and cost to reduce backlog; Greene will follow up

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to headcount by trade, what would it take to maintain a work order backlog in NITRA Section 9 portfolio?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So right now we are maintaining the backlog because it has not increased.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And that's with our 1,700 skilled trades right now.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I can give you a breakdown by craft if you're interested or follow up.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you can get us that and also to what would it cost to get the work under work order backlog from where it is now down to $200,000 and maintained over a five-year period?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Chair, we will definitely follow up with that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But I do want to note one thing that's very important is that work quarters are not just numbers on a page.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Work quarters are actually physically doing the work.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And so the most important thing, for example, that we've started in the past.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I get that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yeah, past couple of years is the relocation programs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Because a lot of work that we have to do, most notably, as a gentleman on the panel just said earlier, asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: You know, asbestos is something that we have advocated for in the past couple of years to get hundreds of millions of dollars in funding to do asbestos, not only in vacant apartments to make them asbestos safe and remove the old tiles, but also in occupied apartments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But what that requires is a resident really making a significant change.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They have to make a decision to move either to a hotel or to another unit while we do those significant repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we want to get repairs done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're looking for funding to do that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: But logistically, a lot of this is also working hand in hand with residents.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm on the ground every day as, you know, every day as well.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm at properties every single day to make sure that we are pushing these cases as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: There is logistical challenges.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how converting 30,000 Section 9 units to PAC has affected overall work order performance. Beck says PAC data is collected differently and is not directly comparable, but PACT has brought $10 billion in investment across over 32,000 apartments.
chapters.title: Banks asks how PAC conversions affect work order performance; Beck says data not comparable

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right, so we're going to move on to transparency.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How has the conversions of the 30,000 Section 9 units to PAC impacted overall work order performance?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You want me to react to you?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It's a little difficult for us to answer just because we, again, on the PAC side, are monitoring work orders as they're resolved in those key pillar areas.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And the work order data and information that we collect on the Section 9 side is vastly different and much more detailed.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And a lot of that is because...

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We are in an oversight role as the Section 8 administrator for the PACT program.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And I think fundamentally, we are able to address the full capital needs that are needed at the developments when they convert through the program.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that's $10 billion in investment that we've been able to make across the city, over 32,000 apartments.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And we can see from the data in that portfolio from the work order data that we collect, you know, that there are significantly fewer work orders opened.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Again, that's for a different subset of key pillar areas.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: But this year so far, there have been 16,000 work orders opened across the 32,000 apartments.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that's about 51 work orders per 100 units or one work order for every two apartments.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It's a very different data set than the NYCHA data set, and I don't think it's fair to compare those two as it's just fundamentally on different footing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'm going to ask this question anyway.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are PAC developments outperforming work order response times at Section 9 developments?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I can speak just to the work order and the response times for the PACT property managers, and they are responding within the vastly, or majority of them are responding within the required response times.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How are they outperforming?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I don't think that is a fair comparison to make.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks why NYCHA publishes only one year of Section 9 work order data rather than data from 2019 onward. Greene says he will check the policy and notes NYCHA shared about 7.5 million work order records with the Council.
chapters.title: Banks asks why only one year of Section 9 data is published; Greene will check policy

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The NITRA metric shows only one year of work order data for Section 9.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Why does NITRA not publish that data from 2019 to today?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'll have to go back and check to see what the policy decision was, but we do have other data available.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And as I said, we have no issue with being transparent and sharing work order data.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For example, we've just shared, again, about seven points.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: 0.5 million work orders with the council that they are free to go through.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We also have a lot of other data portals, for example, on lead, on mold, that share information about the different programs that we have on a program basis.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when it comes to PAC data,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: being published.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When will the PAC data be published at the same level or detailed as Section 9?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So in 2023, we started to publish the monthly reporting data on our website on a quarterly basis.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And that's because we collect it on a monthly basis from each of the properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It will not compare and we will never have the same level of data or detail as the Section 9 side because we are not in that property management role.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We're collecting information across a number of different private property managers across a number of different properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And so what we do publish is the most standardized data set for that entire portfolio.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about NYCHA's oversight of PAC work orders and whether PAC partners follow HUD or Baez standards. Beck says PAC reporting exceeds federal requirements, uses monthly reporting, HQS inspections, compliance monitoring, and independent mold and data analysts.
chapters.title: Banks asks about PAC oversight, software, and closure procedures; Beck describes reporting and analysts

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you describe NYCHA's oversight process for assuring compliance and performance of work orders for the PAC developments?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And are PAC partners required to follow the HUD and the buyer's consent decree standards for work order response times as NYCHA is?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I certainly can.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And just to back up a little bit, the requirements and oversight that we have for reporting from our PAC partners go above and beyond any federal requirement and above and beyond the requirements

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: from HUD for the RAD program.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And, you know, we monitor their performance as private property managers and in a way that no other private property manager is required to report to a city agency.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So it is a very unique circumstance where we're collecting this information on their performance.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: But we do it because we know it's important for the program to perform and live up to its expectations.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And we have these very important HUD pillar areas.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And that's why we've decided to monitor performance and resolution in those key areas to make sure that our teams are responsive.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So we have a couple of different ways we do that.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: One is the reporting information that we collect from teams on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Our leased housing department also helps oversee the administration of the program.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: They conduct those HQS inspections to make sure that the apartments are in good repair.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And our compliance department also monitors work order closeout and does on-site monitoring of our partners.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And all of this is to ensure that they are meeting the expectations that are outlined in the control agreement in our ground lease.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We also review all of their capital plans and their mold capital plans to make sure that the upfront capital investment that's done at the property is getting to the root as it's needed.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So our partners report to us on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We have never missed a report from a team from that monthly reporting process.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And then we go through a data integrity exercise where we review and ensure that all the information shared in that report is complete.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So information is given back to our partners kind of in real time to share any errors or data fixes that need to happen.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We also, as we've been talking about, have the bias agreement for the packed properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And this is where our monthly reporting goes to an independent mold analyst and that independent data analyst.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Those are court appointed analysts.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So that's why they maintain their independence.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Those.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Work orders are then inspected at each property.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: There's a statistically significant number of inspections that are required to happen each month.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And they're ensuring, just as you were describing earlier, that the work that's completed for each of those work orders is actually completed.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And they provide reports on that, those inspections, to the special master.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me just...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We were joined by Councilmember Julie Wan.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let's get that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NYCHA require any specifications as to the kind of software the PAC partners use to manage work orders?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a very fair question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think each of our PAC partners makes their own business decision on the software that they want to use.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And as long as they are able to communicate work order closure data to us and conduct their monthly reporting, we do not determine or require a specific software.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, do you require a PAC partner to follow a specific work order closure procedures?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Each of our work order areas has a timeline associated for resolution.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And those are set by the HUD pillar areas and are aligned with NYCHA's.

chapters.summary: Banks notes PAC on-time work order resolution fell to 74.5% in 2025 from higher rates in prior years and asks whether managers are struggling. Beck says the PAC portfolio has grown rapidly and managers are handling capital repairs simultaneously; she also says NYCHA remains responsible until the conversion date during a 12-to-18-month pre-development period.
chapters.title: Banks notes PAC on-time resolution dropped and asks about pre-development responsibility

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to the percentage of work orders resolved on time at the PAC developments, the average, I believe, is 74.5% of the time.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And this was in the time of 2025 compared to 87.5% of the time in 2024 and 90.75% in this.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: time in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are PAC property managers struggling to address work orders as more and more developments are converted?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think there's a couple layers to that, if I can just give some context.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think what happens

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: or has happened over the past couple of years is the portfolio of the number of units that have converted has grown.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So now we're up to over 32,000 apartments.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: All of those apartments, when they convert into the Section 8 portfolio, have a significant amount of capital needs that are needed in them.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And there is an immediate influx of work and work orders that is handed to the property manager while they're in the middle of completing the capital repairs.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So those two things are happening essentially at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: They must resolve the work orders even while they're...

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: You know, trying to work through an entire replacement of the boiler system.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So sometimes the repair and resolution time is not met, certainly.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And you can see online there are percentages where the on-time resolution is not 100%.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And that's because they are working through those larger capital investments at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When a development is converted to Rad Pack,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Once the conversion takes place, and this is not after all the leases are signed or you meet your threshold to the amount of leases that are needed to be signed,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: who's responsible for the day-to-day operations or for the existing repair issues?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: During that process leading up to when the rehab starts?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So when we select a partner team, we call that pre-development, and that's a process that we're doing with the resident leaders at each of our sites.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So they are working with us to interview and select property managers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So during pre-development, who's responsible for maintaining the property?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: NYCHA is responsible up until the day that we convert, and then immediately after the next day is when the PACT partner property manager...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So up until the day you convert, meaning...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The first community engagement meeting?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: No, there's a date.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or the actual signing of the leases?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: There's a conversion date for each of the properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So as an example...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how far is the conversion date from the community engagement meetings?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It can vary based on the development and the amount of engagement work that happens.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: But we call that period the pre-development period, the engagement period.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: That can last 12 to 18 months or it can last up to two years.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So during that 12 to 18 months or two years, NITRA is responsible for maintaining the property.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA tracks PAC work orders open longer than 100 days and how OCC response compares. Beck says 65 PAC work orders were open more than 100 days through August, and OCC intake from PAC properties is very low, with only 39 tickets in the last quarter.
chapters.title: Banks asks about PAC work orders over 100 days and OCC response

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NYCHA have a process to track work orders that have been opened for longer than 100 days in the PAC sites?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how many such work orders are there in PAC sites and weren't in 2026?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We can track.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Again, we would know.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Oh, let me just look at this really quick.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So through the end of August, which was our last reporting period, we have 65 work orders that have been open for more than 100 days across the PAC portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So again, that's across 32,000 units.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So it accounts for less than half a percent.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to the finance, how do response times from work orders submitted to the OCC center compared to those that are not?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Can you ask that one more time?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How do response times for work orders submitted to the OCC center or to the OCC compared to those that are not?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I guess that's across.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yeah, both PACT and NYCHA, Section 9, have access to the OCC.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: What we've seen on the PACT portfolio side is that the OCC,

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: has pretty low intake from the packed properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So in the last quarter of reporting from the OCC, there were only 39 tickets opened.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: With an average?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: For the packed properties.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: For the packed properties.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: Yeah, and of those...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: He said 39 tickets.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: 39 in total.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And that was in what year?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: This last quarter.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This last.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: So quarter two.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: The last complete.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And do you have any data going back?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: We would have that data and we can get that to you.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: It's reported to the special master at every quarterly report.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: But again, that 39 tickets is less than 1% of the entire packed portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And we have seen pretty low usage.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: of the OCC across the PACT program.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: And we have tried to ensure there's a lot of outreach and information sharing about the OCC, including having the OCC call tenants directly who have had mold and leak work orders.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The OCC is obviously responsible for promoting

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: or advertising its information to the residents in Rad Pack.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: The OCC along with our partners and along with NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think it's a shared responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how do completion rates for work orders submitted to the OCC compare to those that are not?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I don't have that analysis in front of me, but we can look into that.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how recent Critical Repairs Initiative investments have improved work order responses. Greene says NYCHA received funding about two months ago and is still building the program with stakeholders, so it has not launched or had an impact yet.
chapters.title: Banks asks how CRI has improved responses; Greene says program has not launched yet

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How have recent investments in the critical repair initiative improved responses to work orders?

utterances.speaker: Heather Beck
utterances.text: I think I'll turn that over to Dan.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We are still engaging with stakeholders for the rollout of the CRI program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We just received the funding approximately two months ago, and we are working with stakeholders now to build out that program and hope to launch it very shortly.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have not seen an impact yet because it has not started.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there any data that shows the amount of units that would qualify or that would fall under?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: There's not, there's our work order data.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So some subset.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The existing data that you have for work orders, what's a percentage or what's a raw number that would qualify?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I can't give you that math off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I apologize, but it would be born from the numbers that we've been talking about.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: A lot of the CRI program is going to be based on folks who've been waiting too long for cabinets, folks who've been waiting too long for floors, and things that need additional coordination and effort to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the CRI program, again, was building off of programs that we were already doing, like maintenance cares, to prioritize these urgent repairs, missing cabinets.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So there's been no orders.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: There's been no work orders that have been submitted to the CRI.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It hasn't launched yet.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It hasn't launched yet.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: No, it hasn't launched yet.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many elevators have been repaired with FY2027 funding for elevator doors and parts. Keith Grossman says NYCHA has not received the funding yet, so zero elevators have been repaired through that round, though the upgrade takes about half a day to a day.
chapters.title: Banks asks about elevator funding; Grossman says zero elevators repaired because funds not received

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And for fiscal year 2027 budget, the added $2 million over the next three years to support the purchase of elevator door parts and staffing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many elevators have been repaired using this funding?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: I'm going to refer this one to EVP Keith Grossman, who oversees elevators and who's walking up to the table right now and he'll give you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before the council members and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Sorry, I was actually helping a resident.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'll react to the question.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I thought you were going to take it easy on you today, so it's not a tough question.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You do good.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Fiscal year 2027 budget added $2 million over the next three years to support the purchase of elevator doors and parts.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many elevators have been repaired using this funding?

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Again, we just received the funding in the same line as the CRI.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how many elevators are there?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: With this current...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If you can break down the developments that would qualify or fall.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: So this is a I'll preface this by saying the.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Notion of the program is something that we've spoken about a number of times.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Investing in preventative maintenance of our aging assets, right?

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: The average elevator age in NYCHA is 25 years, which is about five years, five to 10 years past their useful life.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Upgrading the operator head, which is what this is, MOVFR, it's a waterproof.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: High tension operator.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: That older unit is a large point of failure for us.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: So we requested funding through the housing plan, and we've graciously accepted it.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: As far as how many have we repaired through this round of funding?

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Zero.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Zero.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Because we haven't gotten the funding yet.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: It's not in our account yet.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there, I mean, would you step out and give us an anticipation?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When would you anticipate getting the funding?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And then moving forward with making these critical repairs.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Soon, it would be the best answer I could give you.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: And as soon as we have the funding, we can start because the actual.

utterances.speaker: Keith Grossman
utterances.text: Repair is the actual it's a it's an upgrade of the existing equipment and it doesn't it takes about a half day to a day.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many mold and leak complaints have been outstanding more than 100 days. Greene says about 12,500 mold tickets and 30,000 leak tickets are pending over 100 days, and the blitz has already addressed 3,000 work orders while targeting developments with trades on site.
chapters.title: Banks asks about mold/leak blitz and 100-day complaints; Greene reports 12,500 mold and 30,000 leak tickets

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: OK, the fiscal year 2027 executive budget also added five million

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: to support a mold and leaks blitz over fiscal years 2027 and 2028.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many mold and leak complaints have been outstanding for more than 100 days?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So in terms of aging, for 100-plus days on the mold side, it's about 12,500.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: On the leak side, pending more than 100 days,

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's about 30,000 that have been pending more than 100 days.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So what we're doing for that program, which has already started, we've already addressed 3,000 work orders through that program.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So it's trades, it's plumbers, plasters, painters, and planners to do those, carpenters as well, to do those comprehensive repairs.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So what we do is we use the data and we target developments and we sit those trades at the developments until we bring down the backlog.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we started as Soda Mayor.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We then moved to Whitman and Ingersoll and Red Hook.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And now we've moved the team into Manhattan at Baruch, Jefferson and Wagner.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Our goal is to bring down the overall work orders by about 10,000 through that initiative of the ones that are open as of that 100 days when they get to those developments.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And the city funding will allow us to extend that funding.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's currently funded with HUD funding, which is time limited, but this will supplement it.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And if it's a successful initiative, we hope it will continue.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how relocating NYCHA staff after PAC conversions affects work order completion times. Greene says staff are moved into existing vacancies, keeping headcount the same, and that filling those vacancies should improve maintenance response times.
chapters.title: Banks asks how PAC staff relocations affect completion times; Greene says staff fill vacancies

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And you've previously indicated that as a development goes through the PAC conversion, staff...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: are relocated to other developments, what impact has this had on work order completion times?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It hasn't really impacted work order completion times because we, number one, we have seen some work orders improve in terms of their completion times and generation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So with the increase of staff, it hasn't?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The staff has not, so the staff are used to fill existing vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So when staff are transitioned, they're moving.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So if it's filling existing vacancies, that means you have, you're adding more bodies to the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So that means there should be, productivity should go up.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Let me step back and let me step back.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So at the development level, so for maintenance workers and for caretakers who are the ones predominantly affected by the PAC conversion, they are moved to open vacant lines.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And there's pretty high turnover at those positions.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they're moved into vacant lines.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Sometimes they're held as a floater while we move them into a permanent personnel line.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But I'm talking about overall.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there an improvement?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Once a conversion takes place and that staff then is transferred over or relocated to another NITRA development.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Well, they're moved to where there's a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, for example, like if a development...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Again, if you're filling a vacancy, right?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The headcount is the same.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: The headcount is still the same.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the service level will be about the same because we're getting back to the base headcount by filling the vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Sometimes we will have additional staff for a short period of time while they await a vacancy to be open to move to that permanent line.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And during that time where we have to go full.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I mean, the responsibility of nature when it comes, you know, with that particular development, it's...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It's giving over the pack.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That body now moves, or those bodies now move over to a NITRA development.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It did no impact at all to the services to the residents or response time, nothing.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Let me, again, so for the staff who are mainly impacted, which are the maintenance workers and the trades, they're moving into an existing vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: For example, right now, I have about 30 maintenance vacancies open.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So when a development closes, these maintenance workers will be moved to fill in those vacancies.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That will make those developments that they're moving to whole.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So right now they're operating with less staff.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now they're going to have back to their original staff.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So that will improve.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Certainly, like, for example, Castle Hill right now.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It will improve.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That will improve.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, that will improve.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And it will also.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So what will it improve?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let's get clarity on that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: It's going to improve response to the maintenance work order.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
