utterances.text: So we'll bring down the response time on the maintenance work orders because we are making a hole, but that's what the headcount is budgeted for.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're not increasing the headcount at that other development to bring, for example, we're not going up from like five to 10 maintenance workers.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We're bringing them back to five, what they're budgeted for.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: On the trade side, we will have more, the trades will have that advantage.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So the trades will have less apartments to respond to.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And I think we're going to see over the next couple of years, the benefit of the trade.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So we would see.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So being close to 30,000, I mean, developments or units have been converted over the pack.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Have you seen an impact or improvement across Niger with the transferring over of labor?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: See, I have seen an improvement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So, yes, I have seen an improvement, but it's not a transfer over.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: What it is is, again, we move the staff to a vacancy.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they're not getting any additional staff.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They're filling their vacancies with that staff that's been.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But when that body's not there.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That means there's jobs that are completed.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So once that vacancy is filled, it's an addition to the work.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just want to clarify on that.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Yes, that we agree.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: And then also, I think we'll start to see our trades have benefit.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Now, on the other side of that, I do want to note.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We do have a new important obligation, which is now we are inspecting every apartment every year, which we should not lose sight of because that is generating more work orders than we've ever seen before.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: 0.5 million work orders because of those inspections.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether NYCHA plans to hire additional staff to address the outstanding work order backlog. Greene says NYCHA hired 47 trades through the MLR program, added lead abatement staff, and is targeting mold and leak work orders through specific programs.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA will hire more staff for backlog; Greene cites MLR hires and lead abatement

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So does NYCHIP plan to hire any additional staff to address the outstanding work order backlog?

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have hired it through the MLR.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Through the MLR, we have hired 47 additional staff.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: We've also positioned staff with our lead abatement program so that they can be more self-sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So they can address, for example, now they've moved up 20,000 abatements.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: They're moving back residents in under 14 days for their abatements, which is a big improvement.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have added trades to specific programs to improve response times, particularly on Molden Leak.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: That was a big program that we worked with the monitor.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: So we have that program designed now to attack these aging work orders and developments that are overwhelmed by them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Daniel Greene
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sophia Fenn says she is a legal fellow at New York Legal Assistance Group's Public Housing Justice Project representing NYCHA tenants with repair issues. She describes tickets mysteriously closed, unproductive inspections, out-of-order repairs, no-show closures, and repeated relocations for asbestos and lead remediation.
chapters.title: Sophia Fenn describes broken NYCHA repair system from legal aid perspective

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Greetings, Chair Banks and members of the New York City Committee on Public Housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify regarding my experiences with NYCHA's work order practices.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: For the past two years, I have worked as a legal fellow at New York Legal Assistance Group on the Public Housing Justice Project, where I work exclusively with NYCHA tenants who are dealing with repair issues in their apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: I have litigated these cases in every housing court in New York City across all five boroughs, including Red Hook Community Justice Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: My experience in this work echoes what many tenants have told you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: The NYCHA work order and repair system is broken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Tenants put in tickets only for those tickets to be mysteriously closed, or if a worker does respond, the visit is not productive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Workers show up five, six, many times to inspect, wherein they just take a picture and leave, only for tenants to be told that no one can find those pictures, and that another date has to be scheduled for more pictures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: All the while, they are living with leaks, pest infestations, destroyed floor tiles, and other conditions that are dangerous to health and safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: When NYCHA does begin repairs, poor project management results in repairs not being completed or being unnecessarily dragged out, placing a significant emotional and physical burden on our clients, and frankly on NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: NYCHA schedules work out of order.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Painters coming before plaster, plaster coming before plumbing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: NYCHA workers come at random times with no warning, even if a scheduled appointment exists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: And if the tenants do not happen to be home, NYCHA will permanently close the ticket as a no-show, restarting the entire process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Other times, clients with significant environmental concerns, such as asbestos and lead, find themselves having to relocate multiple times for remediation because NYCHA is unable to coordinate the two remediations to ensure they happen consecutively.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: I have an elderly client who was relocated for asbestos, had her possessions lost and furniture broken, only to be moved back home and told she also required a lead abatement and would have to be relocated again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: She lived out of boxes for months while waiting for the second relocation to be scheduled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Both relocations were incredibly taxing and negatively impacted her health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Poor systems like these waste the already limited resources of NYCHA maintenance, costing both tenants and NYCHA unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: Increased transparency is also needed regarding NYCHA's inspections and repair records.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: During HP actions, NYCHA can rarely produce details or documentation regarding inspections they conducted or even repair work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: They claim to have made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: An internal record of repair work should be consistently available to tenants so tenants can understand what is going on and avoid the constant runaround from management regarding the repairs in their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophia Fenn
utterances.text: We urge the city and NYCHA to take this opportunity to create policies and practices that model how to maintain and provide housing that is humane and habitable for New Yorkers.

summary: The Committee on Public Housing held an oversight hearing on work order practices at NYCHA and PACT developments, chaired by Council Member Chris Banks.
Public witnesses, legal aid attorneys, and residents described delayed repairs, closed-out tickets, PAC transition confusion, asbestos and lead concerns, and repeated follow-up burdens.

NYCHA officials reported high work order volumes, a 282,000 skilled-trade backlog, improved HUD inspection scores, and new initiatives like Maintenance Cares and CRI, while council members pressed for accountability and faster repairs.
